Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: The energy released when gaseous ions form a crystal depends on the attraction between the ions, which grows with the product of their charges and falls as the ions get larger. The ions in MgO and NaF are of similar size (all have the neon configuration), but the charge product is 4 for MgO and 1 for NaF, so MgO has a much larger lattice enthalpy. R explains A.
steps: A: MgO (2+, 2−) vs NaF (1+, 1−), similar ionic sizes → MgO much larger → true
R: lattice enthalpy rises with ionic charge → true and explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Since the sizes are similar, the difference in charge is the reason for the difference, so R is the correct explanation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', ionic or electrovalent bond: lattice enthalpy
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following molecules has zero dipole moment even though its central atom carries lone pairs of electrons?

solution.concept: Dipole moment, shape and lone pairs
solution.explanation: XeF₄ has two lone pairs on xenon placed opposite each other (trans) in the octahedral arrangement, so the molecule is square planar: the four Xe–F bond dipoles cancel in pairs and the two lone pairs also cancel. Its dipole moment is zero.
steps: XeF₄: AB₄E₂ → square planar, symmetric → μ = 0
NH₃ (pyramidal), SF₄ (see-saw), ClF₃ (T-shaped) are unsymmetrical → μ ≠ 0
solution.why_others_wrong: NH₃, SF₄ and ClF₃ also carry lone pairs, but their shapes are unsymmetrical, so their bond dipoles do not cancel.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', VSEPR theory; dipole moment
solution.final_answer: Option C: XeF₄

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A process is called reversible when:

options.text: it takes place rapidly in one step against a constant external pressure
no heat is exchanged between the system and the surroundings
it is carried out infinitesimally slowly, so that the system stays practically in equilibrium with the surroundings at every stage and its direction can be reversed by an infinitesimal change
the temperature of the system remains constant throughout

solution.explanation: NCERT describes a reversible process as one carried out so slowly, through a series of infinitesimal steps, that the system is always almost in equilibrium with the surroundings; reversing an infinitesimal change of a variable reverses the process. Real processes, which go at a finite rate, are irreversible.
steps: Reversible = infinitesimally slow, quasi-equilibrium at every stage
One-step expansion against a constant pressure is irreversible
solution.why_others_wrong: No heat exchange defines an adiabatic process and constant temperature an isothermal one; either can be reversible or irreversible. A rapid one-step change is irreversible.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', work: reversible and irreversible processes
solution.final_answer: Option C: it is carried out infinitesimally slowly, so that the system stays practically in equilibrium with the surroundings at every stage and its direction can be reversed by an infinitesimal change

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A gas absorbs 250 J of heat, and its internal energy increases by 100 J. The work done BY the gas on the surroundings is:

solution.concept: First law of thermodynamics, ΔU = q + w
solution.explanation: In the IUPAC convention, q is positive for heat absorbed and w is the work done on the system. The work done by the system is −w.
steps: ΔU = q + w → 100 = 250 + w → w = −150 J (work done on the gas)
Work done by the gas = −w = +150 J
solution.why_others_wrong: 350 J adds q and ΔU. −150 J is the work done on the gas, not by it. −350 J combines both slips.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics
solution.final_answer: Option A: 150 J

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following equations represents the standard enthalpy of formation of methanol, CH₃OH(l)?

solution.explanation: ΔfH° refers to the formation of ONE mole of a compound from its elements in their most stable states (reference states) at 1 bar: carbon as graphite, hydrogen and oxygen as H₂(g) and O₂(g).
steps: Elements in reference states: C(graphite), H₂(g), O₂(g)
solution.why_others_wrong: Diamond is not the reference state of carbon. CO is a compound, not an element. The last equation forms two moles, so its ΔH is 2ΔfH°.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', standard enthalpy of formation
solution.final_answer: Option B: C(graphite) + 2H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → CH₃OH(l)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Gibbs energy is an intensive property.
Statement II: A negative value of ΔG for a reaction tells us that the reaction is feasible, but not how fast it will take place.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: G = H − TS is an extensive property and a state function, so Statement I is false. ΔG < 0 at constant temperature and pressure means the process is spontaneous (thermodynamically feasible), but thermodynamics says nothing about the rate; that is the subject of chemical kinetics. Statement II is true.
steps: I: G depends on the amount of substance → extensive → false
II: thermodynamics gives feasibility, kinetics gives rate → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false because G, like H and S, is extensive; Statement II is a point NCERT makes at the start of chemical kinetics.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', Gibbs energy and spontaneity; Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', introduction
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: When 0.10 mol of a salt dissolves in water in an insulated constant-pressure (coffee-cup) calorimeter, 100 g of solution is formed and its temperature falls by 2.0 K. Taking the specific heat of the solution as 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and neglecting the heat capacity of the calorimeter, the enthalpy of solution of the salt is:

solution.concept: Measuring ΔH at constant pressure: q_p = ΔH
solution.explanation: The temperature falls, so the dissolution absorbs heat from the solution: the process is endothermic. The heat absorbed is mcΔT, and dividing by the moles dissolved gives the molar enthalpy of solution.
steps: q = m c ΔT = 100 × 4.18 × 2.0 = 836 J absorbed by the dissolving salt
ΔsolH = +836 J / 0.10 mol = +8360 J mol⁻¹ = +8.36 kJ mol⁻¹
solution.why_others_wrong: −8.36 kJ mol⁻¹ has the wrong sign: a fall in temperature means an endothermic process. +0.836 is the total heat in kJ without dividing by the moles. +83.6 divides by 0.010 mol.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', measurement of ΔU and ΔH: calorimetry
solution.final_answer: Option C: +8.36 kJ mol⁻¹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The reaction 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) is carried out at a constant pressure and 300 K. Treating the gases as ideal and neglecting the volume of the liquid, the work done ON the system when 2 mol of H₂ reacts completely is (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: Pressure–volume work in a reaction involving gases
solution.explanation: At constant pressure, w = −pΔV = −Δn(g)RT. Three moles of gas disappear, so the surroundings compress the system and the work done on it is positive.
solution.why_others_wrong: −7.48 kJ is the sign of work done BY the system. +4.99 kJ uses Δn = −2, counting only H₂. +2.49 kJ uses Δn = −1.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', work, enthalpy and the relation ΔH = ΔU + Δn(g)RT
solution.final_answer: Option D: +7.48 kJ

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For an ideal gas, the molar heat capacity at constant pressure, C_p, is greater than the molar heat capacity at constant volume, C_v.
Reason (R): At constant pressure part of the heat supplied is used by the gas to do work of expansion against the surroundings, so more heat is needed for the same rise in temperature.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: At constant volume all the heat raises the internal energy (q_v = ΔU = C_vΔT). At constant pressure the gas also expands and does work pΔV = RΔT per mole, so q_p = C_vΔT + RΔT and C_p − C_v = R. R explains A.
steps: A: C_p > C_v; for an ideal gas C_p − C_v = R → true
R: extra heat at constant pressure goes into expansion work → true and explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the physical origin of the relation C_p − C_v = R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', heat capacity: relation between C_p and C_v for an ideal gas
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The enthalpy change for C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g) equals the sum of the enthalpy changes for C(graphite) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g) and CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g).
Statement II: The standard enthalpy of combustion of graphite is numerically equal to the standard enthalpy of formation of CO₂(g).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Hess's law of constant heat summation
solution.explanation: Because enthalpy is a state function, the enthalpy change from graphite and O₂ to CO₂ is the same whether the change happens in one step or through CO; Statement I is true. Burning one mole of graphite, the reference state of carbon, in O₂ forms one mole of CO₂ from its elements, so ΔcH°(graphite) = ΔfH°(CO₂, g); Statement II is true.
steps: I: one-step ΔH = sum of the two-step ΔH values (Hess's law) → true
II: C(graphite) + O₂ → CO₂ is both combustion of graphite and formation of CO₂ → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', Hess's law of constant heat summation; enthalpy of combustion
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
For four reactions at 300 K (take 2.303RT = 5.74 kJ mol⁻¹), match List-I (standard Gibbs energy change, ΔrG°) with List-II (equilibrium constant, K).

List-I:
A. −11.48 kJ mol⁻¹
B. 0
C. +5.74 kJ mol⁻¹
D. −5.74 kJ mol⁻¹

List-II:
I. 1
II. 10
III. 0.1
IV. 100

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: ΔrG° = −2.303RT log K, so log K = −ΔrG°/(2.303RT). A negative ΔrG° gives K > 1, zero gives K = 1 and a positive value gives K < 1.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes reverse the sign relation (a positive ΔrG° giving K > 1) or mix up 10 and 100.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', Gibbs energy change and equilibrium
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For a reaction, ΔH° = −35.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = −40 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, both independent of temperature. Its equilibrium constant at 300 K is (take 2.303RT = 5.75 kJ mol⁻¹ at 300 K):

solution.concept: ΔG° from ΔH° and ΔS°, then K from ΔG°
solution.explanation: First find ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° (with ΔS° in kJ), then use ΔG° = −2.303RT log K.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 × 10⁻⁴ drops the minus sign in ΔG° = −2.303RT log K. 1.5 × 10⁸ adds TΔS° instead of subtracting it (ΔG° = −47 kJ). 4 is log K, not K.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', Gibbs energy change and equilibrium
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1 × 10⁴

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Using the following data (kJ mol⁻¹), the standard enthalpy of formation of methane, C(graphite) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g), is:
Enthalpy of atomisation of graphite, C(graphite) → C(g): 717
Bond dissociation enthalpy of H–H: 436
Mean C–H bond enthalpy in methane: 416

solution.concept: Enthalpy of formation from atomisation and bond enthalpies (Hess's law)
solution.explanation: Go from the elements to gaseous atoms (atomise graphite, break two H–H bonds), then form four C–H bonds. Energy absorbed in the first step is positive; energy released in forming bonds is negative.
solution.why_others_wrong: −792 kJ mol⁻¹ leaves out the atomisation of graphite. −511 kJ mol⁻¹ breaks only one H–H bond. +75 kJ mol⁻¹ has the sign reversed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', enthalpy of atomisation; bond enthalpy; Hess's law
solution.final_answer: Option D: −75 kJ mol⁻¹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
For the reaction 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), ΔH° = −571.6 kJ at 298 K. Treating the gases as ideal, which of the following statements are correct? (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

(a) The standard enthalpy of formation of H₂O(l) is −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹.
(b) ΔU° for the reaction as written is about −564.2 kJ.
(c) ΔU° for the reaction is more negative than ΔH°.
(d) The entropy of the system decreases in this reaction.
(e) ΔH° for 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) is −571.6 kJ.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: ΔH, ΔU and entropy for a reaction involving gases
solution.explanation: ΔfH° refers to one mole: −571.6/2 = −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH = ΔU + Δn(g)RT with Δn(g) = −3, so ΔU = ΔH + 3RT = −571.6 + 7.4 = −564.2 kJ, which is less negative than ΔH. Three moles of gas become liquid, so the entropy of the system falls. The reverse reaction has ΔH° = +571.6 kJ.
steps: (e) reversing a reaction reverses the sign of ΔH → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) or (e) are wrong, and (a) and (d) only leaves out the true statement (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', enthalpy, ΔH = ΔU + Δn(g)RT, and standard enthalpy of formation
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a reaction with ΔH° = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = +80 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (both independent of temperature), the equilibrium constant at 400 K is less than 1.
Statement II: For the same reaction, the equilibrium constant at 500 K is equal to 1.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Temperature, ΔG° and the equilibrium constant
solution.explanation: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°. At 400 K, ΔG° = 40 − 32 = +8 kJ mol⁻¹ > 0, so K < 1. At 500 K, ΔG° = 40 − 40 = 0, so log K = 0 and K = 1. Both statements are true; above 500 K K exceeds 1.
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements follow directly from ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° and ΔG° = −2.303RT log K.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', Gibbs energy and spontaneity; Gibbs energy change and equilibrium
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A 10% (volume/volume) solution of ethanol in water contains 10 mL of ethanol dissolved in 100 mL of water.
Statement II: A solution of 35% (v/v) ethylene glycol in water is used as an antifreeze in the cooling systems of cars, because it lowers the freezing point of water.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Volume percentage; an application of freezing-point depression
solution.explanation: Volume percentage = volume of component/total volume of SOLUTION × 100. A 10% (v/v) ethanol solution has 10 mL of ethanol in 100 mL of solution, not in 100 mL of water, so Statement I is false. NCERT notes that 35% (v/v) ethylene glycol is used as an antifreeze in cars; it lowers the freezing point of water to about 255.4 K. Statement II is true.
steps: I: 10 mL ethanol per 100 mL of solution → false as written
II: ethylene glycol antifreeze lowers the freezing point → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I uses 100 mL of solvent instead of 100 mL of solution.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', expressing concentration of solutions: volume percentage
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The osmotic pressure of a 0.05 M aqueous solution of sucrose (a non-electrolyte) at 27 °C is (R = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹):

solution.explanation: For a dilute solution of a non-electrolyte, π = CRT with C in mol L⁻¹ and T in kelvin.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.46 atm uses i = 2, but sucrose does not dissociate. 0.111 atm uses 27 instead of 300 K. 12.3 atm takes the concentration as 0.5 M.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', osmosis and osmotic pressure
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1.23 atm

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Assuming complete dissociation, the van't Hoff factor of potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II), K₄[Fe(CN)₆], in dilute aqueous solution is:

solution.concept: van't Hoff factor of an ionic solute
solution.explanation: The complex ion stays intact in solution: K₄[Fe(CN)₆] → 4K⁺ + [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, giving five ions per formula unit, so i = 5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 counts only the K⁺ ions. 11 breaks the complex ion into Fe²⁺ and six CN⁻, which does not happen. 2 treats it like a 1 : 1 salt.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', abnormal molar masses: van't Hoff factor
solution.final_answer: Option C: 5

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For an ideal solution of two volatile liquids A and B at a fixed temperature, the plot of the total vapour pressure against the mole fraction of A is:

options.text: a straight line parallel to the composition axis
a straight line joining p°B (at x_A = 0) and p°A (at x_A = 1)

solution.concept: Raoult's law for a solution of two volatile liquids
solution.explanation: p_total = p°B + (p°A − p°B) x_A, which is linear in x_A. At x_A = 0 it equals p°B and at x_A = 1 it equals p°A.
steps: p_total = x_A p°A + (1 − x_A) p°B = p°B + (p°A − p°B) x_A → linear
solution.why_others_wrong: A maximum or a minimum appears only for non-ideal solutions with positive or negative deviations. A horizontal line would need p°A = p°B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', vapour pressure of liquid–liquid solutions: Raoult's law
solution.final_answer: Option D: a straight line joining p°B (at x_A = 0) and p°A (at x_A = 1)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Liquids A and B form an ideal solution. At a certain temperature p°A = 600 mm Hg and p°B = 200 mm Hg. For the vapour in equilibrium with the solution to contain equal mole fractions of A and B, the mole fraction of A in the liquid must be:

solution.concept: Composition of the vapour over an ideal solution (Raoult's and Dalton's laws)
solution.explanation: The mole fraction of A in the vapour is y_A = p_A/p_total = x_A p°A/(x_A p°A + x_B p°B). Equal mole fractions in the vapour means the partial pressures are equal: x_A p°A = x_B p°B.
steps: Check: p_A = p_B = 150 mm Hg → y_A = 0.5
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.50 assumes the liquid has the same composition as the vapour. 0.75 interchanges p°A and p°B. 0.33 is just the ratio p°B/p°A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', vapour pressure of liquid–liquid solutions
solution.final_answer: Option A: 0.25

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 100 mL of a 0.1 M aqueous solution of urea is mixed with 100 mL of a 0.2 M aqueous solution of glucose. Assuming the volumes are additive, the osmotic pressure of the mixture at 300 K is (R = 0.082 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: Osmotic pressure of a mixture of non-electrolytes
solution.explanation: Osmotic pressure depends on the total molar concentration of solute particles. Both solutes are non-electrolytes, so add their moles and divide by the total volume.
steps: Moles: urea 0.010 + glucose 0.020 = 0.030 mol in 0.200 L → C = 0.15 M
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.38 atm adds the two molarities without allowing for dilution. 2.46 atm and 4.92 atm use only one solute's original concentration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', osmosis and osmotic pressure
solution.final_answer: Option C: 3.69 atm

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The molarity of an aqueous solution decreases slightly when the solution is warmed.
Reason (R): The volume of the solution increases with temperature, while the amount of solute in it stays the same.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution. Warming expands the solution, so the same number of moles is spread over a larger volume and the molarity falls. Molality, mass percentage and mole fraction do not change, as they involve only masses. R explains A.
steps: A: M = n/V and V rises with T → M falls → true
R: V increases, n unchanged → true and explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: R gives exactly the reason why molarity depends on temperature.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', expressing concentration of solutions
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
For 0.1 m aqueous solutions of the following solutes, assuming complete dissociation of the electrolytes (K_f of water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹), which statements are correct?

(a) The van't Hoff factor of Al₂(SO₄)₃ is 5.
(b) The van't Hoff factor of MgSO₄ is 2.
(c) The van't Hoff factor of urea is 1.
(d) The depression of freezing point of the CaCl₂ solution is 0.372 K.
(e) Of the solutions of Al₂(SO₄)₃, MgSO₄, urea and CaCl₂, the MgSO₄ solution has the lowest freezing point.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: van't Hoff factor and depression of freezing point
solution.explanation: Al₂(SO₄)₃ → 2Al³⁺ + 3SO₄²⁻ (i = 5); MgSO₄ → Mg²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ (i = 2); urea does not ionise (i = 1); CaCl₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ (i = 3). ΔT_f = i K_f m, so CaCl₂ gives 3 × 1.86 × 0.1 = 0.558 K, and the solution with the largest i, Al₂(SO₄)₃, freezes lowest.
steps: (e) largest i is Al₂(SO₄)₃ (5) → it has the lowest freezing point → false
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.372 K uses i = 2 for CaCl₂, and (e) ignores that Al₂(SO₄)₃ gives the most particles.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', abnormal molar masses: van't Hoff factor
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Benzoic acid (C₆H₅COOH, molar mass 122 g mol⁻¹) partly dimerises in benzene: 2C₆H₅COOH ⇌ (C₆H₅COOH)₂. Its molar mass found from the depression of the freezing point of a dilute benzene solution is 203.3 g mol⁻¹. The percentage of benzoic acid molecules that are dimerised is:

solution.concept: Degree of association from the van't Hoff factor
solution.explanation: i = normal molar mass / observed molar mass. For dimerisation, if a fraction α of the molecules associates, the particles per original molecule are (1 − α) + α/2 = 1 − α/2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40% takes α = 1 − i, forgetting that two molecules make one dimer. 60% is i itself. 20% is 1 − α.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', abnormal molar masses: association of ethanoic acid and benzoic acid in benzene
solution.final_answer: Option D: 80%

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: An aqueous solution of glucose (molar mass 180 g mol⁻¹) is 10% by mass. Its freezing point is (K_f of water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹; freezing point of water = 0 °C):

solution.concept: Freezing-point depression from a mass percentage
solution.explanation: Take 100 g of solution: 10 g of glucose in 90 g of water. Convert to molality and use ΔT_f = K_f m.
solution.why_others_wrong: −1.03 °C uses 100 g (the solution) instead of 90 g of water. −0.10 °C takes 10 g of glucose in 1 kg of water. +1.15 °C forgets that the freezing point is lowered.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', depression of freezing point
solution.final_answer: Option A: −1.15 °C

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Liquids A and B form an ideal solution; at temperature T, p°A = 400 mm Hg and p°B = 100 mm Hg. The vapour in equilibrium with a solution containing equal numbers of moles of A and B is removed and condensed completely. The vapour pressure of this condensate at the same temperature T is:

solution.concept: Vapour composition over an ideal solution and repeated vaporisation
solution.explanation: First find the composition of the vapour, which is richer in the more volatile A. The condensate is a liquid of that composition, and Raoult's law then gives its vapour pressure.
steps: Original liquid: p_A = 0.5 × 400 = 200, p_B = 0.5 × 100 = 50, total 250 mm Hg
solution.why_others_wrong: 250 mm Hg is the vapour pressure of the original solution. 320 mm Hg leaves out B's contribution. 400 mm Hg is the vapour pressure of pure A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', vapour pressure of liquid–liquid solutions
solution.final_answer: Option C: 340 mm Hg

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
A 0.1 m aqueous solution of a weak monobasic acid HA is 10% ionised (HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻). Which of the following statements are correct? (For water, K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹ and K_b = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹.)

(a) The van't Hoff factor of HA in this solution is 1.1.
(b) The depression of freezing point is about 0.205 K.
(c) The elevation of boiling point is 0.052 K.
(d) The solution contains fewer solute particles per kilogram of water than a 0.1 m solution of NaCl (completely dissociated).
(e) The van't Hoff factor of HA is greater than 2.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: van't Hoff factor of a partly ionised solute
solution.explanation: For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ with degree of ionisation α, particles per formula unit = (1 − α) + 2α = 1 + α = 1.1. Colligative properties are multiplied by i: ΔT_f = 1.1 × 1.86 × 0.1 = 0.205 K and ΔT_b = 1.1 × 0.52 × 0.1 = 0.0572 K. NaCl gives i = 2, more particles than HA (i = 1.1).
steps: (c) 0.0572 K, not 0.052 K (that ignores i) → false
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.052 K forgets the van't Hoff factor; (e) is false since a 1 : 1 weak acid cannot exceed i = 2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', abnormal molar masses: van't Hoff factor
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The total vapour pressure of a mixture of acetone and chloroform is lower than the value predicted by Raoult's law.
Reason (R): Chloroform molecules form hydrogen bonds with acetone molecules, so the attractions between unlike molecules are stronger than those between like molecules, which reduces the escaping tendency of both components.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: On mixing, a chloroform molecule hydrogen-bonds to the oxygen of an acetone molecule. These A–B interactions are stronger than the A–A and B–B interactions they replace, so fewer molecules escape into the vapour and the vapour pressure is below the ideal value (negative deviation). R explains A.
steps: A: acetone–chloroform shows negative deviation → true
R: stronger A–B attraction via hydrogen bonding lowers vapour pressure → true and explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the molecular reason NCERT gives for the negative deviation of this mixture.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', non-ideal solutions
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A little sugar containing radioactive carbon is added to a saturated solution of ordinary sugar that is in contact with undissolved sugar at constant temperature. After some time, radioactivity is found both in the solution and in the undissolved solid sugar. This shows that:

options.text: the solubility of sugar increases with time
dissolution and crystallisation continue at equal rates, i.e. the equilibrium is dynamic
radioactive sugar is more soluble than ordinary sugar
the solution is no longer saturated

solution.explanation: At equilibrium the concentration of the saturated solution stays constant, but molecules keep leaving the solid and returning to it at the same rate. That is how radioactive sugar molecules end up in the solid as well as in the solution.
steps: Rate of dissolution = rate of crystallisation
Exchange of molecules → radioactivity in both phases
solution.why_others_wrong: The concentration of a saturated solution is constant at a fixed temperature, so the solubility does not change and the solution stays saturated. Labelled and ordinary sugar have the same solubility.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', solid–liquid equilibrium: dynamic nature of equilibrium
solution.final_answer: Option B: dissolution and crystallisation continue at equal rates, i.e. the equilibrium is dynamic

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Aquatic species are more comfortable in cold water than in warm water.
Reason (R): The Henry's law constant (K_H) of oxygen in water increases with rise in temperature, so less oxygen dissolves in warm water.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Henry's law and the effect of temperature on gas solubility
solution.explanation: By Henry's law, p = K_H x. A larger K_H at a higher temperature means a smaller mole fraction x of the gas in solution at the same partial pressure. Warm water therefore holds less dissolved oxygen, which is why aquatic animals are more comfortable in cold water. R explains A.
steps: A: more dissolved O₂ in cold water → true
R: K_H rises with T → solubility of O₂ falls → true and explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: NCERT links these two facts directly in its discussion of Henry's law.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', solubility of a gas in a liquid: Henry's law
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a polyprotic acid such as H₂CO₃, the first ionisation constant is larger than the second (K_a1 > K_a2).
Statement II: It is more difficult to remove a proton from a negatively charged ion such as HCO₃⁻ than from a neutral H₂CO₃ molecule.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT notes that the higher-order ionisation constants of a polyprotic acid are smaller than the lower-order ones, because the positively charged proton is harder to remove from an anion that already carries negative charge than from a neutral molecule. Both statements are true.
steps: I: K_a1 > K_a2 > K_a3 for polyprotic acids → true
II: electrostatic attraction of the anion holds the proton more strongly → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true; Statement II is in fact the reason for Statement I.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', di- and polybasic acids
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The solubility product of a sparingly soluble salt MX₂, which dissolves as MX₂(s) ⇌ M²⁺(aq) + 2X⁻(aq), is 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ at 298 K. Its molar solubility in water at 298 K is:

solution.concept: Molar solubility from K_sp for an AB₂-type salt
solution.explanation: If s mol L⁻¹ dissolves, [M²⁺] = s and [X⁻] = 2s, so K_sp = s(2s)² = 4s³.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.66 × 10⁻⁶ treats the salt as AB-type (s = √K_sp). 3.17 × 10⁻⁴ takes the cube root of K_sp without the factor 4. 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ is [X⁻] = 2s, not the solubility.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', solubility product constant
solution.final_answer: Option C: 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When the equilibrium mixture C(s) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂(g) is compressed to a smaller volume at constant temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the backward direction.
Reason (R): Compressing the mixture increases the equilibrium constant K_p of this reaction.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Effect of pressure on a heterogeneous gaseous equilibrium
solution.explanation: Counting only gases, the forward reaction turns 1 mol of gas into 2 mol. Raising the pressure by compression favours the side with fewer moles of gas, so the equilibrium shifts backward; A is true. K_p depends only on temperature, so compression does not change it; R is false. The shift happens because the reaction quotient becomes larger than K_p.
steps: A: Δn(g) = +1, compression favours fewer gas moles → backward → true
R: K changes only with temperature → false
solution.why_others_wrong: The shift is explained by Le Chatelier's principle (Q_p > K_p after compression), not by any change in K_p.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', effect of pressure change; factors affecting equilibria
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 2.0 mol of SO₂ and 1.5 mol of O₂ are heated in a closed 2.0 L vessel. At equilibrium, 1.2 mol of SO₃ is present: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g). The value of K_c at this temperature is:

solution.concept: Equilibrium constant from initial amounts and the amount of product
solution.explanation: Use the stoichiometry to find the equilibrium amounts, convert them to concentrations with the vessel volume, and substitute in K_c = [SO₃]²/([SO₂]²[O₂]).
steps: SO₃ formed = 1.2 mol → SO₂ used = 1.2 mol, O₂ used = 0.6 mol
At equilibrium: SO₂ = 0.8 mol, O₂ = 0.9 mol, SO₃ = 1.2 mol
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.33 ignores the squares in the expression. 2.5 uses amounts in moles instead of concentrations. 15 subtracts all 1.2 mol from the O₂, ignoring the 2 : 1 ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', equilibrium constant and its calculation
solution.final_answer: Option D: 5.0 L mol⁻¹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The pH of an aqueous solution of ammonium acetate at 298 K is practically independent of its concentration.
Reason (R): For a salt of a weak acid and a weak base, pH = 7 + ½(pK_a − pK_b), an expression that contains no concentration term.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Hydrolysis of a salt of a weak acid and a weak base
solution.explanation: Both NH₄⁺ and CH₃COO⁻ hydrolyse. NCERT gives pH = 7 + ½(pK_a − pK_b) for such a salt, which depends only on the two ionisation constants, so diluting the solution does not change its pH appreciably. R explains A.
steps: A: pH of CH₃COONH₄ solution does not depend on c → true
R: pH = 7 + ½(pK_a − pK_b) has no c → true and explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: The concentration cancels out because both ions hydrolyse; R states this result.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', hydrolysis of salts and the pH of their solutions
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about 0.1 M aqueous solutions at 298 K are correct?

(a) A solution of (NH₄)₂SO₄ is acidic.
(b) A solution of Na₂CO₃ is basic.
(c) A solution of KNO₃ has pH 7.
(d) A solution of NaCl is acidic.
(e) A solution of CH₃COOK is acidic.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Acidic, basic and neutral salt solutions
solution.explanation: A salt of a strong acid and a weak base, such as (NH₄)₂SO₄, gives an acidic solution because NH₄⁺ hydrolyses. Salts of weak acids with strong bases, such as Na₂CO₃ and CH₃COOK, give basic solutions because the anion hydrolyses. Salts of a strong acid and a strong base, such as KNO₃ and NaCl, do not hydrolyse and are neutral.
steps: (a) NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺ → acidic → true
(b) CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ → basic → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) are wrong, and (a) and (b) only misses the true statement (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', hydrolysis of salts and the pH of their solutions
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (gaseous equilibrium) with List-II (relation between K_p and K_c).

List-I:
A. N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)
B. N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
C. H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
D. PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) ⇌ PCl₅(g)

List-II:
I. K_p = K_c
II. K_p = K_c(RT)
III. K_p = K_c(RT)⁻¹
IV. K_p = K_c(RT)⁻²

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: K_p = K_c(RT)^Δn, where Δn = (moles of gaseous products) − (moles of gaseous reactants) in the balanced equation.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes take Δn as reactants minus products, or mix up −1 and −2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', relationship between K_p and K_c
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A buffer of pH 5.74 is to be made from acetic acid and sodium acetate at 298 K. The ratio [CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH] needed is (pK_a of CH₃COOH = 4.74):

solution.concept: Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer
solution.explanation: pH = pK_a + log([salt]/[acid]), so log([CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH]) = pH − pK_a.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.1 inverts the ratio (acid/salt). 1 gives pH = pK_a = 4.74. 100 corresponds to pH 6.74.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', buffer solutions
solution.final_answer: Option B: 10

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The ionisation constants of four acids at 298 K are: HF 6.8 × 10⁻⁴, HCOOH 1.8 × 10⁻⁴, CH₃COOH 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ and HCN 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁰. Which of the following is the strongest base?

solution.concept: Strengths of conjugate acid–base pairs, K_a × K_b = K_w
solution.explanation: For a conjugate pair, K_a × K_b = K_w, so the weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base. HCN has the smallest K_a, so CN⁻ has the largest K_b (about 2 × 10⁻⁵).
steps: Smallest K_a (HCN) → largest K_b → CN⁻ is the strongest base
solution.why_others_wrong: F⁻, HCOO⁻ and CH₃COO⁻ are conjugate bases of stronger acids, so they are weaker bases than CN⁻.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', relation between K_a and K_b
solution.final_answer: Option C: CN⁻

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: At 298 K, a solution of pH 8 has [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ mol L⁻¹.
Statement II: At any temperature, an aqueous solution in which [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] is neutral.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: At 298 K, pH + pOH = 14, so pH 8 means pOH 6 and [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol L⁻¹; it is [H₃O⁺] that equals 10⁻⁸ mol L⁻¹. Statement I is false. Neutrality means [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻], whatever the temperature; only the pH of a neutral solution changes with temperature because K_w changes. Statement II is true.
steps: II: definition of a neutral solution → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I gives [H₃O⁺] instead of [OH⁻].
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', ionisation of water and the pH scale
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Silver nitrate solution is added drop by drop to a solution that is 0.010 M in Cl⁻ and 0.010 M in CrO₄²⁻ at 298 K. K_sp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ and K_sp(Ag₂CrO₄) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹². Ignoring the volume change, which salt precipitates first, and at what [Ag⁺] does it begin to precipitate? (√1.1 = 1.05)

solution.explanation: A salt starts to precipitate when its ionic product reaches K_sp. Find the [Ag⁺] needed for each salt; the one needing the smaller [Ag⁺] precipitates first. Note the square in K_sp(Ag₂CrO₄) = [Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻].
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ M forgets to take the square root for Ag₂CrO₄. 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ M is the solubility of AgCl in pure water, ignoring the 0.010 M Cl⁻. 1.05 × 10⁻⁵ M is where Ag₂CrO₄ starts, which is later.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', solubility product; common ion effect on solubility
solution.final_answer: Option D: AgCl first, at [Ag⁺] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁸ M

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 50 mL of 0.2 M aqueous ammonia (NH₄OH) is mixed with 50 mL of 0.2 M HCl at 298 K. The pH of the resulting solution is (pK_b of NH₄OH = 4.74; log 2 = 0.30):

solution.concept: pH at the equivalence point of a weak base–strong acid reaction (salt hydrolysis)
solution.explanation: Equal amounts of NH₄OH and HCl react completely to give NH₄Cl, the salt of a weak base and a strong acid, in 100 mL. NH₄⁺ hydrolyses, and pH = 7 − ½pK_b − ½log c.
steps: n(NH₄OH) = n(HCl) = 0.010 mol → 0.010 mol NH₄Cl in 0.100 L → c = 0.10 M
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.98 forgets that mixing halves the concentration (uses c = 0.2 M). 4.13 subtracts ½ log c with the wrong sign. 8.87 uses the formula for the salt of a weak acid and a strong base.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', hydrolysis of salts and the pH of their solutions
solution.final_answer: Option B: 5.13

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following mixtures acts as a buffer solution?

options.text: 50 mL of 0.1 M NH₄OH + 50 mL of 0.1 M HCl
50 mL of 0.1 M CH₃COOH + 60 mL of 0.1 M NaOH
50 mL of 0.1 M NH₄OH + 25 mL of 0.1 M HCl
50 mL of 0.1 M HCl + 50 mL of 0.1 M NaCl

solution.concept: Preparing a buffer by partial neutralisation
solution.explanation: A buffer needs a weak acid with its salt, or a weak base with its salt. Half-neutralising NH₄OH with HCl leaves equal amounts of NH₄OH and NH₄Cl, which is a basic buffer.
steps: 5.0 mmol NH₄OH + 2.5 mmol HCl → 2.5 mmol NH₄OH + 2.5 mmol NH₄Cl → buffer
solution.why_others_wrong: Equal amounts of NH₄OH and HCl leave only NH₄Cl. 6.0 mmol NaOH with 5.0 mmol CH₃COOH leaves excess strong base and no weak acid. HCl with NaCl is a strong acid with its salt, which does not buffer.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', buffer solutions
solution.final_answer: Option C: 50 mL of 0.1 M NH₄OH + 25 mL of 0.1 M HCl

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
For the equilibrium C(s) + CO₂(g) ⇌ 2CO(g), ΔH > 0, set up in a closed vessel, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) K_p = p²(CO)/p(CO₂).
(b) K_p = K_c(RT).
(c) Adding more solid carbon at constant volume and temperature shifts the equilibrium in the forward direction.
(d) Raising the temperature increases the equilibrium constant.
(e) Compressing the mixture to a smaller volume at constant temperature increases the amount of CO at equilibrium.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Heterogeneous equilibrium: K_p expression, K_p–K_c relation and Le Chatelier's principle
solution.explanation: A pure solid does not appear in the equilibrium constant, so K_p = p²(CO)/p(CO₂). Δn(g) = 2 − 1 = +1, so K_p = K_c(RT). Adding carbon changes nothing because its 'concentration' is constant. For an endothermic reaction, K increases with temperature. Compression favours the side with fewer gas moles, so CO decreases.
steps: (c) pure solid does not shift the equilibrium → false
(d) endothermic → K rises with T → true
(e) compression shifts backward → CO decreases → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) or (e) are wrong, and (b) and (d) only leaves out the true statement (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', heterogeneous equilibria; relation between K_p and K_c; Le Chatelier's principle
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The ionic product of water at 323 K is K_w = 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴. The pH of a 1.0 × 10⁻³ M aqueous solution of NaOH at 323 K, assuming complete dissociation, is (log 5.5 = 0.74):

solution.concept: pH of a strong base when K_w is not 10⁻¹⁴
solution.explanation: pH + pOH = pK_w at any temperature. At 323 K, pK_w is less than 14, so a base of given [OH⁻] has a lower pH than it would at 298 K.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.00 uses pK_w = 14, valid only at 298 K. 11.74 adds log 5.5 instead of subtracting it. 6.63 is the pH of pure (neutral) water at 323 K.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', ionisation of water; the pH scale
solution.final_answer: Option A: 10.26

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A molar conductivity of 1 S cm² mol⁻¹ is equal to:

solution.explanation: Since 1 m = 100 cm, 1 m² = 10⁴ cm², so 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m². Therefore 1 S cm² mol⁻¹ = 10⁻⁴ S m² mol⁻¹.
steps: 1 S cm² mol⁻¹ = 10⁻⁴ S m² mol⁻¹
solution.why_others_wrong: 10⁻² converts a length, not an area. 10² and 10⁴ convert in the wrong direction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', measurement of the conductivity of ionic solutions; molar conductivity
solution.final_answer: Option D: 1 × 10⁻⁴ S m² mol⁻¹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The oxidation numbers of the two nitrogen atoms in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, are:

solution.concept: Oxidation numbers in a compound with two different ions
solution.explanation: Treat the ions separately. In NH₄⁺: x + 4(+1) = +1 → x = −3. In NO₃⁻: x + 3(−2) = −1 → x = +5.
solution.why_others_wrong: +1 and +1 is the average (sum zero shared over two atoms), which hides the two different environments. −3 and +3, and +3 and +5, miscalculate one of the ions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Redox Reactions', oxidation number
solution.final_answer: Option C: −3 and +5

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the dry (Leclanché) cell, manganese is reduced at the cathode.
Reason (R): In the cathode reaction MnO₂ + NH₄⁺ + e⁻ → MnO(OH) + NH₃, the oxidation state of manganese changes from +4 to +3.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Electrode reactions of the dry cell
solution.explanation: Reduction is a decrease in oxidation number. In MnO₂, Mn is +4. In MnO(OH), with O = −2 and H = +1, x + (−2) + (−2) + 1 = 0 gives x = +3. The gain of one electron by each Mn at the carbon cathode is the reduction stated in A. R explains A.
steps: Decrease in oxidation number → reduction at the cathode
solution.why_others_wrong: R shows the change in oxidation state that makes the cathode process a reduction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', batteries: primary batteries (dry cell); Class 11 Chemistry, 'Redox Reactions', oxidation number
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (cell) with List-II (its description).

List-I:
A. Dry (Leclanché) cell
B. Lead storage battery
C. Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell
D. Daniell cell

List-II:
I. Reactants are fed in continuously, and the energy of combustion of the fuel is converted directly into electrical energy
II. Zinc and copper electrodes in solutions of their ions; standard emf 1.1 V
III. Primary battery: its reaction occurs only once, and it cannot be recharged
IV. Secondary battery: it can be recharged by passing a current through it in the opposite direction

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The dry cell is a primary battery; after use it cannot be recharged. The lead storage battery is a secondary battery and is recharged by reversing the current. A fuel cell converts the energy of combustion of fuels such as hydrogen directly into electrical energy, with reactants supplied continuously. The Daniell cell uses Zn and Cu electrodes and has E° = 1.1 V.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange primary and secondary batteries, or the fuel cell with the Daniell cell.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', batteries and fuel cells; galvanic cells
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In a basic solution, permanganate ion oxidises iodide ion to iodine and is itself reduced to manganese dioxide: MnO₄⁻(aq) + I⁻(aq) → MnO₂(s) + I₂(s). When the ionic equation is balanced with the smallest whole numbers (using H₂O and OH⁻), the coefficients of I⁻ and OH⁻ are respectively:

solution.concept: Balancing a redox equation in basic medium (half-reaction method)
solution.explanation: Mn goes from +7 to +4 (gains 3 e⁻) and I from −1 to 0 (loses 1 e⁻ per I⁻). Balance the half-reactions in basic medium and multiply to equalise the electrons.
steps: Check: charge −8 on each side; O 12 = 12; H 8 = 8
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 and 16 come from the acidic-medium equation (MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺, with 16H⁺). 4 is the coefficient of H₂O, not OH⁻. 3 is the coefficient of I₂, not I⁻.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Redox Reactions', balancing of redox reactions: half-reaction method
solution.final_answer: Option C: 6 and 8

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the conductivity of electrolytic (ionic) solutions are correct?

(a) It depends on the nature of the electrolyte added.
(b) It depends on the size of the ions produced and their solvation.
(c) It depends on the nature of the solvent and its viscosity.
(d) It decreases as the temperature of the solution increases.
(e) It is due to the movement of electrons through the solution.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT lists the factors on which the conductivity of electrolytic solutions depends: the nature of the electrolyte, the size of the ions and their solvation, the nature of the solvent and its viscosity, the concentration and the temperature. Ionic conductance is due to the movement of ions, and it increases with rising temperature.
steps: (d) ionic conductance increases with temperature → false
(e) charge is carried by ions, not electrons → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) describes metallic conduction, and (e) confuses electronic with electrolytic conduction; (a) and (b) only misses the true statement (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', conductance of electrolytic solutions
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At 298 K, the reduction potential of a hydrogen electrode with p(H₂) = 1 bar becomes more negative as the pH of its solution increases.
Reason (R): For this electrode, the Nernst equation gives E = −0.059 pH volt at 298 K.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Nernst equation for the hydrogen electrode
solution.explanation: For H⁺(aq) + e⁻ → ½H₂(g), E = E° − 0.059 log(p(H₂)^½/[H⁺]) = 0 + 0.059 log[H⁺] = −0.059 pH at 298 K with p(H₂) = 1 bar. As pH rises, E falls (becomes more negative). R explains A.
steps: pH 1 → −0.059 V; pH 7 → −0.413 V: more negative
solution.why_others_wrong: R gives the quantitative relation from which A follows.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', Nernst equation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Given the standard reduction potentials E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V, E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, E°(Ni²⁺/Ni) = −0.25 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, which of the following ions can oxidise Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ under standard conditions?

solution.concept: Predicting redox reactions from electrode potentials
solution.explanation: An ion can oxidise Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ under standard conditions only if its own reduction potential is higher than that of Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ (+0.77 V), so that E°cell is positive.
steps: Cu²⁺: 0.34 − 0.77 < 0; Ni²⁺ and Zn²⁺ even more negative → not feasible
solution.why_others_wrong: Cu²⁺, Ni²⁺ and Zn²⁺ all have reduction potentials below +0.77 V, so the reaction would have a negative E°cell.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', electrode potential and the electrochemical series
solution.final_answer: Option A: Ag⁺

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: During the discharge of a lead storage battery, PbO₂ at the cathode is oxidised.
Statement II: During the charging of a lead storage battery, sulphuric acid is consumed.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Reactions in the lead storage battery
solution.explanation: During discharge, Pb at the anode is oxidised (0 → +2) and PbO₂ at the cathode is REDUCED (+4 → +2), both forming PbSO₄ and consuming H₂SO₄. Charging reverses this: PbSO₄ is converted back to Pb and PbO₂ and sulphuric acid is regenerated, not consumed. Both statements are false.
steps: I: PbO₂ (+4) → PbSO₄ (+2) is a reduction → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I mistakes the cathode reduction for an oxidation; Statement II describes discharge, not charging.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', secondary batteries: lead storage battery
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (condition for a cell) with List-II (what it implies about the cell reaction at that temperature).

List-I:
A. E°cell > 0
B. E°cell < 0
C. E°cell = 0
D. E_cell = 0

List-II:
I. ΔrG° = 0 and K = 1
II. The cell reaction has reached equilibrium (Q = K)
III. ΔrG° < 0 and K > 1
IV. ΔrG° > 0 and K < 1

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Relations among E°cell, ΔrG°, K and E_cell
solution.explanation: ΔrG° = −nFE°cell and ΔrG° = −RT ln K. A positive E°cell gives a negative ΔrG° and K > 1; a negative E°cell gives K < 1; E°cell = 0 gives ΔrG° = 0 and K = 1. E_cell (not E°) becomes zero when the cell is fully discharged, i.e. the reaction is at equilibrium and Q = K.
solution.why_others_wrong: The trap is to treat E°cell = 0 and E_cell = 0 as the same condition; one is about standard states, the other about the actual mixture reaching equilibrium.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', equilibrium constant from the Nernst equation; electrochemical cell and Gibbs energy
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Calculate the emf at 298 K of the cell Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq, 0.1 M) || H⁺(aq, pH = 2) | H₂(g, 1 bar) | Pt, whose cell reaction is Zn(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + H₂(g). (E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V; 2.303RT/F = 0.059 V)

solution.concept: Nernst equation for a cell with a hydrogen electrode
solution.explanation: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0 − (−0.76) = +0.76 V. Two electrons are transferred, and E_cell = E°cell − (0.059/2) log([Zn²⁺] p(H₂)/[H⁺]²).
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.85 V adds the correction (Q inverted). 0.73 V forgets to square [H⁺]. 0.58 V uses 0.059 instead of 0.059/2 for a two-electron reaction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', Nernst equation
solution.final_answer: Option D: 0.67 V

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Consider the balanced equation 2MnO₄⁻ + 5H₂O₂ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5O₂ + 8H₂O. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) H₂O₂ acts as a reducing agent.
(b) The oxidation number of oxygen in H₂O₂ changes from −1 to 0.
(c) Each MnO₄⁻ ion gains five electrons.
(d) A total of five electrons is transferred in the reaction as written.
(e) The coefficient of H⁺ in the balanced equation would be 16 if it were written correctly.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Oxidising and reducing agents; electron count in a balanced redox equation
solution.explanation: Mn goes from +7 in MnO₄⁻ to +2 in Mn²⁺, a gain of 5 electrons per ion, so MnO₄⁻ is the oxidising agent. Oxygen in H₂O₂ (−1) goes to O₂ (0), losing 1 electron per O atom, 2 per H₂O₂, so H₂O₂ is the reducing agent. As written, 2 × 5 = 10 electrons are transferred (5 H₂O₂ × 2). The equation is already balanced with 6H⁺: charge +4 on both sides, O 18 = 18, H 16 = 16.
steps: (a) O.N. of O rises → H₂O₂ is oxidised → reducing agent → true
(e) the given equation with 6H⁺ is balanced; 16H⁺ belongs to the oxalate reaction → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) counts the electrons for one MnO₄⁻ only, and (e) recalls the coefficient from a different reaction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Redox Reactions', redox reactions in terms of oxidation number; balancing of redox reactions
solution.final_answer: Option C: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The equilibrium constant of a cell reaction in which two electrons are transferred is 1 × 10²⁰ at 298 K. The standard Gibbs energy change of the reaction is (2.303RT/F = 0.059 V; F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹):

solution.explanation: First find E°cell from log K = nE°cell/0.059, then ΔrG° = −nFE°cell.
solution.why_others_wrong: −56.9 kJ mol⁻¹ uses n = 1 in ΔrG° = −nFE°. −227.7 kJ mol⁻¹ forgets to divide by n when finding E° (taking E° = 0.059 × 20 = 1.18 V). +113.9 kJ mol⁻¹ has the wrong sign for K > 1.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', equilibrium constant from the Nernst equation; electrochemical cell and Gibbs energy
solution.final_answer: Option B: −113.9 kJ mol⁻¹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, the reaction at the anode is O₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻(aq).
Statement II: The dry (Leclanché) cell has a potential of about 2.0 V.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Electrode reactions and potentials of commercial cells
solution.explanation: In the H₂–O₂ fuel cell, oxidation takes place at the anode: 2H₂(g) + 4OH⁻(aq) → 4H₂O(l) + 4e⁻. The reaction O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ is a reduction and occurs at the cathode, so Statement I is false. NCERT gives the dry cell a potential of nearly 1.5 V, so Statement II is false too.
steps: I: the reaction quoted is a reduction → cathode, not anode → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are false: Statement I swaps the electrodes and Statement II gives the wrong potential.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', primary batteries; fuel cells
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The hydrogenation of ethene, C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g), has the experimentally found rate law rate = k[C₂H₄]. The overall order of this reaction is:

solution.concept: Order of reaction from the rate law
solution.explanation: The order is the sum of the powers of the concentration terms in the experimental rate law, not the sum of the coefficients in the balanced equation. Here only [C₂H₄] appears, to the first power.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 adds the stoichiometric coefficients of the balanced equation, which do not decide the order. 0 and 3/2 do not match the rate law.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', order of a reaction; first-order reactions
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (rate law) with List-II (unit of the rate constant, concentration in mol L⁻¹ and time in s).

List-I:
A. Rate = k
B. Rate = k[A]
C. Rate = k[A]^½[B]^(3/2)
D. Rate = k[A][B]²

List-II:
I. s⁻¹
II. L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
III. mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
IV. L² mol⁻² s⁻¹

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Units of the rate constant for different orders
solution.explanation: For an overall order n, k has units (mol L⁻¹)^(1−n) s⁻¹. Order 0 → mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, order 1 → s⁻¹, order 2 → L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹, order 3 → L² mol⁻² s⁻¹.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the zero- and first-order units, or treat the half-integer powers as a third-order law.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', units of rate constant
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When the temperature is raised, the peak of the kinetic energy distribution curve of the molecules shifts towards higher energy and the curve broadens out.
Statement II: When the temperature is raised, the total area under the distribution curve increases.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution and the effect of temperature
solution.explanation: At a higher temperature the most probable kinetic energy increases, so the peak moves to higher energy, and the curve spreads out, so a greater fraction of molecules has energy above E_a. Statement I is true. The area under the curve represents the total number (or fraction) of molecules, which does not change, so Statement II is false.
steps: I: peak shifts right and the curve broadens → true
II: area = total probability (number of molecules) → constant → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II forgets that the curve only redistributes the same number of molecules over energies.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', temperature dependence of the rate of a reaction
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For a zero-order reaction, a plot of the rate of the reaction against the concentration of the reactant is:

options.text: a straight line through the origin with slope k
a straight line parallel to the concentration axis
a straight line with a negative slope
a curve that rises steeply and then levels off

solution.explanation: For a zero-order reaction, rate = k[R]⁰ = k, so the rate does not depend on concentration: the plot is a horizontal line at height k.
steps: rate = k, independent of [R] → horizontal straight line
solution.why_others_wrong: A straight line through the origin with slope k is the rate–concentration plot of a first-order reaction. The other shapes do not describe rate = constant.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', zero-order reactions
solution.final_answer: Option B: a straight line parallel to the concentration axis

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
For a reaction R → P at constant temperature, the following data were obtained:
t = 0 min: [R] = 0.80 mol L⁻¹; t = 10 min: [R] = 0.60 mol L⁻¹; t = 20 min: [R] = 0.40 mol L⁻¹.
The order of the reaction and its rate constant are:

options.text: zero order; k = 0.20 mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹
zero order; k = 0.020 mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹

solution.concept: Identifying the order from concentration–time data
solution.explanation: Equal decreases in [R] (0.20 mol L⁻¹) in equal times (10 min) show a constant rate, the mark of a zero-order reaction, [R] = [R]₀ − kt. For a first-order reaction [R] would fall by equal FRACTIONS in equal times, but 0.60/0.80 = 0.75 while 0.40/0.60 = 0.67.
steps: Δ[R] = 0.20 mol L⁻¹ every 10 min → constant rate → zero order
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.0288 min⁻¹ comes from applying the first-order equation to the first interval only; the second interval would give a different k, so the data are not first order. 0.20 mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹ forgets to divide by 10 min. 0.020 min⁻¹ has the right number but the first-order unit.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', integrated rate equations: zero-order reactions
solution.final_answer: Option D: zero order; k = 0.020 mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The reaction 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) has the rate law rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. If the volume of the reaction vessel is suddenly reduced to half at constant temperature, the rate of the reaction becomes:

solution.concept: Effect of concentration on rate through the rate law
solution.explanation: Halving the volume doubles the concentration of every gas. Substitute 2[NO] and 2[O₂] in the rate law.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 times doubles only [NO]. 2 times doubles only [O₂]. 1/8 treats halving the volume as halving the concentrations.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', dependence of rate on concentration: rate law
solution.final_answer: Option C: 8 times the original rate

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a zero-order reaction, each successive half-life is half as long as the one before it.
Reason (R): The half-life of a zero-order reaction, t½ = [R]₀/2k, is directly proportional to the initial concentration of the reactant.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: After one half-life the concentration is [R]₀/2, and this becomes the 'initial' concentration for the next half-life. Since t½ ∝ [R]₀, the second half-life is [R]₀/4k, half of the first, and so on. R explains A.
solution.why_others_wrong: A follows directly from the proportionality stated in R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', half-life of a reaction
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
A reaction A + B → products follows the rate law rate = k[A][B]. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The reaction is of second order overall.
(b) The unit of k is L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ (concentration in mol L⁻¹, time in s).
(c) If B is present in large excess, the reaction behaves as a first-order reaction.
(d) Doubling the concentrations of both A and B makes the rate four times as fast.
(e) The reaction must be an elementary bimolecular reaction.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Order, units of k and pseudo first-order behaviour
solution.explanation: The overall order is 1 + 1 = 2, so k has units L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. With B in large excess, [B] stays almost constant and rate = k′[A] (pseudo first order). Doubling both concentrations multiplies the rate by 2 × 2 = 4. A rate law of this form does not prove that the reaction is elementary; order is found experimentally and a complex reaction can have the same rate law.
steps: (e) the rate law does not establish the mechanism → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (e) is false, so the options containing it are wrong; (a), (b) and (c) only leaves out the true statement (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', order and molecularity; pseudo first-order reactions
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A first-order reaction has an activation energy of 53.6 kJ mol⁻¹ and a half-life of 40 min at 300 K. Assuming the Arrhenius pre-exponential factor is constant, its half-life at 310 K is (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; log 2 = 0.301):

solution.concept: Arrhenius equation combined with the first-order half-life
solution.explanation: Use log(k₂/k₁) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂) to find how much k increases; since t½ = 0.693/k, the half-life falls by the same factor.
solution.why_others_wrong: 80 min multiplies instead of dividing. 40 min ignores the temperature change. 10 min treats the rate constant as increasing four times.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', temperature dependence: Arrhenius equation; half-life of a first-order reaction
solution.final_answer: Option D: 20 min

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For the first-order decomposition 2N₂O₅(g) → 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g), the rates are written as −d[N₂O₅]/dt = k₁[N₂O₅], d[NO₂]/dt = k₂[N₂O₅] and d[O₂]/dt = k₃[N₂O₅]. The relation among k₁, k₂ and k₃ is:

solution.concept: Rates of reaction in terms of different reactants and products
solution.explanation: The rate of reaction is −½ d[N₂O₅]/dt = ¼ d[NO₂]/dt = d[O₂]/dt. Substitute each expression.
solution.why_others_wrong: k₁ = k₂ = k₃ ignores the stoichiometric coefficients. The other two invert the factors (for example, NO₂ is formed twice as fast as N₂O₅ disappears, not half as fast).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', rate of a chemical reaction
solution.final_answer: Option C: 2k₁ = k₂ = 4k₃

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
A first-order reaction has a half-life of 20 min. Which of the following statements are correct? (ln 2 = 0.693; 2.303 log 1000 = 6.909)

(a) Its rate constant is 0.0347 min⁻¹.
(b) 75% of the reactant reacts in 40 min.
(c) 93.75% of the reactant reacts in 60 min.
(d) About 200 min is needed for 99.9% completion.
(e) Doubling the initial concentration doubles the half-life.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Half-life relations for a first-order reaction
solution.explanation: k = 0.693/t½ = 0.0347 min⁻¹. After n half-lives, (½)ⁿ of the reactant remains: two half-lives (40 min) leave 25%, i.e. 75% reacted; three half-lives (60 min) leave 12.5%, i.e. 87.5% reacted. For 99.9% completion, t = 6.909/k ≈ 199 min ≈ 10 half-lives. The half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on the initial concentration.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) or (e) are wrong; (c) counts four half-lives in 60 min, and (e) describes a zero-order reaction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', half-life of a reaction
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A catalyst increases the rate constants of the forward and the backward reactions of a reversible reaction by the same factor.
Reason (R): A catalyst lowers the activation energies of the forward and the backward reactions by the same amount.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Effect of a catalyst on a reversible reaction
solution.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative path whose energy barrier is lower by the same amount for both directions (the energies of reactants and products are unchanged). With k = A e^(−Ea/RT), equal lowering of Ea multiplies both rate constants by the same factor, so their ratio, the equilibrium constant, is unchanged. R explains A.
steps: Ea(f) and Ea(b) both fall by the same ΔE
k_f and k_b both multiplied by e^(ΔE/RT) → K = k_f/k_b unchanged
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the reason the factor is the same; this is also why a catalyst does not change K.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Chemical Kinetics', effect of catalyst
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (scientist) with List-II (contribution to the classification of elements).

List-I:
A. Johann Dobereiner
B. John Newlands
C. Lothar Meyer
D. Henry Moseley

List-II:
I. Plotted atomic volume against atomic weight and obtained a periodically repeating pattern
II. Showed that the frequencies of the characteristic X-rays of the elements vary regularly with their atomic numbers
III. Groups of three elements (triads) in which the atomic weight of the middle element is about the mean of the other two
IV. Law of octaves: every eighth element, in order of atomic weight, resembles the first

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Dobereiner noted triads; Newlands proposed the law of octaves; Lothar Meyer plotted physical properties such as atomic volume against atomic weight and saw periodicity; Moseley's X-ray work showed that atomic number is the more fundamental property, leading to the modern periodic law.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap triads with octaves or Lothar Meyer with Moseley.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', genesis of periodic classification
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text: Mendeleev placed iodine after tellurium in his periodic table, even though iodine has the lower atomic weight. He did this because:

options.text: he arranged the elements strictly in order of increasing atomic number
iodine resembles fluorine, chlorine and bromine in its properties, so it belongs in their group
the atomic weight of tellurium had not yet been measured
iodine and tellurium were both thought to be metals

solution.concept: Mendeleev's periodic table: properties given priority over atomic weight
solution.explanation: Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic weight but gave greater importance to similarities in properties. Where the two conflicted, as for tellurium and iodine, he placed iodine with the halogens it resembles, ignoring the order of atomic weights.
steps: Iodine placed in the group of F, Cl and Br
solution.why_others_wrong: Atomic numbers were introduced only later by Moseley. Both atomic weights were known, and neither element was considered a typical metal.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', Mendeleev's periodic law
solution.final_answer: Option B: iodine resembles fluorine, chlorine and bromine in its properties, so it belongs in their group

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The elements on the extreme left of a period, the alkali metals, show the strongest tendency to lose electrons, i.e. the strongest reducing behaviour in the period.
Statement II: Among the elements of a period other than the noble gas, the halogen on the extreme right shows the strongest tendency to gain electrons, i.e. the strongest oxidising behaviour.
