options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

NCERT also gives wheat, paddy and mango as plants with a single ovule in the ovary (R true). Whether the endosperm is used up depends on embryo development, not on how many ovules the ovary holds, so R does not explain A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In humans, every pregnancy has a 50 per cent chance of producing a male or a female child. A couple plans to have three children. What is the probability that all three will be sons?

solution.concept: Independent chance of a son in each pregnancy
solution.explanation: The father produces X-bearing and Y-bearing sperms in equal proportion, so each pregnancy independently has a probability of 1/2 of being a son. Three sons in a row: 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/2 is the chance for one pregnancy only; 1/6 wrongly divides by 3; 3/8 is the chance of exactly two sons (or exactly one).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', sex determination: sex determination in humans
solution.final_answer: Option D: 1/8

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In the human ABO blood group system, how many of the six possible genotypes give blood group A?

solution.explanation: Iᴬ is dominant over i, so both IᴬIᴬ and Iᴬi produce only sugar A and give blood group A. IᴬIᴮ gives AB, IᴮIᴮ and Iᴮi give B, and ii gives O: six genotypes, four phenotypes.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: On the basis of his observations on monohybrid crosses, Mendel proposed two general rules, today called the first and second laws of inheritance. They are the:

options.text: Law of segregation and law of independent assortment
Law of dominance and law of independent assortment
Law of dominance and law of segregation
Law of linkage and law of segregation

solution.explanation: NCERT: based on his observations on monohybrid crosses, Mendel proposed two general rules, the First Law or Law of Dominance and the Second Law or Law of Segregation. The law of independent assortment came from his dihybrid crosses.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The law of segregation is based on the fact that the alleles do not show any blending and that both the characters are recovered as such in the F2 generation, though one of them is not seen at the F1 stage.
Statement II: The law of independent assortment states that when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, the segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair of characters.

Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When the tall F1 plants of Mendel's monohybrid cross between tall and dwarf pea plants were self-pollinated, some dwarf plants appeared in the F2 generation.
Reason (R): The factor for dwarfness was present in the F1 plants, but it was not expressed because the factor for tallness is dominant.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: In F1 (Tt) the dwarf factor t is carried but masked by the dominant T. During gamete formation the two factors segregate, so F1 plants produce t gametes; when two t gametes meet, tt (dwarf) plants appear in F2 (about one in four). The presence of the unexpressed recessive factor in F1 (R) is why dwarf plants reappear (A).
steps: A: true (about 1/4 of F2 are dwarf)
Hidden t in F1 segregates into gametes → tt in F2: R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of one gene
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In Mendel's dihybrid cross RRYY × rryy, the F1 plants were self-pollinated. What fraction of the F2 plants would be true-breeding for both seed shape and seed colour?

solution.explanation: A plant breeds true for both characters only if it is homozygous at both loci: RRYY, RRyy, rrYY or rryy. Each of these occurs in 1/16 of the F2, so together they make 4/16 = 1/4. (Equivalently, P(homozygous) = 1/2 for each gene, and 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.)
steps: Homozygous at both loci: RRYY, RRyy, rrYY, rryy
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/16 counts only RRYY; 9/16 is the fraction with both dominant traits; 1/2 is the homozygous fraction for one gene only.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of two genes
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1/4

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In the cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc, the three genes assort independently. What fraction of the offspring will be homozygous at all three loci (dominant or recessive)?

solution.explanation: For one gene, Aa × Aa gives AA (1/4), Aa (1/2) and aa (1/4), so the chance of being homozygous (AA or aa) is 1/2. The three genes assort independently, so the chance of being homozygous at all three loci is 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/64 counts only one homozygous genotype (e.g. AABBCC); 27/64 is the fraction showing all three dominant traits; 1/2 is the answer for a single gene.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of two genes: law of independent assortment
solution.final_answer: Option C: 1/8

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A man with blood group A (genotype Iᴬi) marries a woman with blood group B (genotype Iᴮi). What is the probability that their first child will be a daughter with blood group AB?

solution.concept: Combining an autosomal cross with the sex of the child
solution.explanation: Iᴬi × Iᴮi gives IᴬIᴮ, Iᴬi, Iᴮi and ii in equal proportion, so P(blood group AB) = 1/4. The chance that the child is a daughter is 1/2, independently. P(daughter with AB) = 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/4 ignores the sex of the child; 1/2 is the chance of a daughter alone; 3/8 adds instead of multiplying (1/4 + 1/8).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', co-dominance; sex determination in humans
solution.final_answer: Option A: 1/8

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In the F2 generation of Mendel's dihybrid cross RRYY × rryy, consider only the seeds that are round and yellow. How many different genotypes are found among them, and which genotype is the most frequent?

solution.explanation: Round yellow seeds need at least one R and one Y. In the 16-box Punnett square they are RRYY (1), RRYy (2), RrYY (2) and RrYy (4): four genotypes making up 9/16 of the F2. RrYy (4/16) is the most frequent.
solution.why_others_wrong: RRYY is the rarest round-yellow genotype (1/16); nine is the number of F2 genotypes in all; two ignores the RRYy and RrYY classes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of two genes
solution.final_answer: Option D: Four; RrYy

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a person of genotype IᴬIᴬ marries a person of genotype IᴮIᴮ, all their children have blood group AB.
Reason (R): Iᴬ and Iᴮ are co-dominant: when both are present together, each expresses its own type of sugar.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Every child receives Iᴬ from one parent and Iᴮ from the other, so all are IᴬIᴮ. NCERT: when Iᴬ and Iᴮ are present together they both express their own types of sugars, which is co-dominance, and red blood cells carry both A and B sugars, giving blood group AB. R is the reason why IᴬIᴮ children are AB rather than A or B.
steps: R explains why they are AB
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', deviations from Mendelism: co-dominance
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Individuals with Turner's syndrome have 45 chromosomes and those with Klinefelter's syndrome have 47 chromosomes, and individuals with either condition are sterile.
Statement II: Both Turner's syndrome and Klinefelter's syndrome arise from polyploidy.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Turner's syndrome: absence of one X chromosome, 45 with X0; such females are sterile as the ovaries are rudimentary. Klinefelter's syndrome: an additional X chromosome, 47 with XXY; such individuals are sterile (Statement I true). Both involve the gain or loss of a single chromosome, which is aneuploidy; polyploidy is an increase in whole sets of chromosomes caused by failure of cytokinesis (Statement II false).
steps: Turner: 45, X0, sterile; Klinefelter: 47, XXY, sterile → Statement I true
Single-chromosome change = aneuploidy → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', genetic disorders: chromosomal disorders
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (disorder) with List-II (underlying defect).

List-I:
A. Sickle-cell anaemia
B. α-thalassemia
C. Phenylketonuria
D. Down's syndrome

List-II:
I. Reduced synthesis of α-globin due to mutation or deletion of the genes HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16
II. Presence of an additional copy of chromosome 21
III. Substitution of a single base (GAG to GUG) at the sixth codon of the β-globin gene
IV. Lack of the enzyme that converts the amino acid phenylalanine into tyrosine

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Molecular and chromosomal basis of disorders
solution.explanation: Sickle-cell anaemia: a single base substitution GAG → GUG at the sixth codon of the β-globin gene, replacing glutamic acid by valine. α-thalassemia: controlled by two closely linked genes HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16; mutation or deletion reduces α-globin synthesis. Phenylketonuria: the affected individual lacks the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine. Down's syndrome: trisomy of chromosome 21.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the two haemoglobin disorders, or PKU with Down's syndrome, or sickle-cell anaemia with PKU.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', genetic disorders
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about sex determination are correct?

(a) In grasshoppers, the males produce two kinds of sperms: with an X chromosome and without it.
(b) In birds, the sex of the offspring depends on the type of egg that is fertilised.
(c) In Drosophila, the female is heterogametic.
(d) In honey bees, the males produce sperms by mitosis.
(e) In humans, a couple who already have two sons have a lower chance than 50 per cent of having another son.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: (a) True: XO males produce sperms with and without X (male heterogamety). (b) True: in birds the female (ZW) produces Z and W eggs, so the egg decides the sex. (c) False: Drosophila follows the XY type; the male is heterogametic. (d) True: the haploid male bee produces sperms by mitosis. (e) False: each pregnancy has an independent 50 per cent chance of a son.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options including (c) or (e) include a false statement; '(b), (c) and (d)' also omits (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', sex determination
solution.final_answer: Option C: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) In phenylketonuria, a mutation in a single gene shows several phenotypic effects.
(b) Human skin colour, controlled by three genes, is an example of pleiotropy.
(c) In most cases, a pleiotropic gene acts through its effect on metabolic pathways that contribute towards different phenotypes.
(d) In polygenic inheritance, the effect of each allele is additive.
(e) In pleiotropy, a single phenotype is controlled by several genes.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Pleiotropy: a single gene exhibits multiple phenotypic expressions, usually by affecting metabolic pathways; phenylketonuria is NCERT's example ((a) and (c) true). Polygenic inheritance: several genes control one trait, e.g. human skin colour, and the phenotype reflects the additive contribution of each allele ((d) true). So (b) and (e) describe polygenic inheritance, not pleiotropy, and are false.
steps: Polygenic: many genes → one trait, additive (skin colour)
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (b) or (e) mislabel polygenic inheritance as pleiotropy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', deviations from Mendelism: pleiotropy; polygenic inheritance
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A plant heterozygous for two genes (AaBb) is test-crossed with aabb. The 1000 progeny are: 425 Aabb, 425 aaBb, 75 AaBb and 75 aabb. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The two genes are linked; the heterozygous parent had received AB from one parent and ab from the other, and the recombination frequency is 15 per cent
The two genes are linked, and the recombination frequency is 85 per cent
The two genes assort independently, since all four classes appear
The two genes are linked; the heterozygous parent had received Ab from one parent and aB from the other, and the recombination frequency is 15 per cent

solution.explanation: In a test cross, the most frequent classes are the parental (non-recombinant) types. Here Aabb and aaBb (850) are frequent, so the dihybrid carried the combinations Ab and aB. The rare AaBb and aabb (150) are recombinants: recombination frequency = 150/1000 = 15 per cent. Independent assortment would give the four classes in about equal numbers.
steps: Frequent classes = parental: Ab and aB
solution.why_others_wrong: AB/ab would make AaBb and aabb the frequent classes; 85 per cent is the parental fraction, not the recombinant one; independent assortment would give a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', linkage and recombination
solution.final_answer: Option D: The two genes are linked; the heterozygous parent had received Ab from one parent and aB from the other, and the recombination frequency is 15 per cent

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Two unaffected parents have a daughter with sickle-cell anaemia. What is the probability that their next child will be a son affected by sickle-cell anaemia?

solution.concept: Autosomal recessive disorder and sex of the child
solution.explanation: Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosome-linked recessive disorder; only HbˢHbˢ individuals show the disease. An affected child of unaffected parents means both parents are carriers (HbᴬHbˢ). P(affected) = 1/4, P(son) = 1/2, so P(affected son) = 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/4 ignores the sex of the child; 1/2 treats the disorder as if half the children were affected; 1/16 multiplies 1/4 twice.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', genetic disorders: sickle-cell anaemia
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1/8

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A woman is a carrier of haemophilia and is also heterozygous for phenylketonuria (an autosomal recessive disorder). Her husband has normal blood clotting and is also heterozygous for phenylketonuria. The two genes are inherited independently. What is the probability that their first child will be a haemophilic son who also has phenylketonuria?

solution.concept: Combining a sex-linked and an autosomal trait
solution.explanation: Haemophilia: XᴴXʰ × XᴴY gives XᴴXᴴ, XᴴXʰ, XᴴY and XʰY in equal proportion, so P(haemophilic son) = 1/4. Phenylketonuria: Pp × Pp gives pp with probability 1/4. Independent genes: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/32 multiplies by an extra 1/2 for the sex, although the 1/4 already includes it; 1/8 is the probability for a son already known to be male (1/2 × 1/4); 1/4 considers only one of the two disorders.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', Mendelian disorders: haemophilia, phenylketonuria
solution.final_answer: Option D: 1/16

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Suppose a polygenic trait is controlled by three genes A, B and C, and each dominant allele adds an equal amount to the phenotype. Two plants, AABBCC and aabbcc, are crossed and the AaBbCc F1 plants are intercrossed. What fraction of the F2 will match either of the two original parents in phenotype?

solution.concept: Extreme classes of a polygenic trait
solution.explanation: The phenotype depends only on the number of dominant alleles. Only AABBCC has 6 and only aabbcc has 0. For each gene P(AA) = 1/4, so P(AABBCC) = (1/4)³ = 1/64; likewise P(aabbcc) = 1/64. Either extreme: 1/64 + 1/64 = 2/64 = 1/32.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/64 counts only one parental type; 1/16 and 1/8 come from using 1/2 or (1/2)² per gene instead of 1/4.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', polygenic inheritance
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1/32

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A woman of blood group A with normal colour vision has a son who is colour blind and has blood group O. Which of the following men could be the boy's biological father?

options.text: A colour-blind man with blood group AB
A man with normal colour vision and blood group AB
A man with normal colour vision and blood group B
Any of these three men, since the son received both traits from his mother

solution.concept: ABO exclusion combined with X-linked inheritance
solution.explanation: Blood group O is ii, so the son received i from each parent. The mother must be Iᴬi, and the father must carry i; a man with blood group AB (IᴬIᴮ) cannot be the father. Colour blindness in a son comes from his mother's X chromosome (she is a carrier), since he receives only the Y from his father; the father's vision therefore gives no information. A man of blood group B (genotype Iᴮi) could be the father.
steps: Son ii: father must carry i → AB excluded
Son's X (and colour blindness) from mother → father's vision irrelevant
solution.why_others_wrong: Both AB men cannot supply i; the son's blood group O needs an i from the father, so it is not true that any man could be the father.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', co-dominance; sex-linked inheritance: colour blindness
solution.final_answer: Option C: A man with normal colour vision and blood group B

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A colour-blind woman married to a man with normal colour vision can have sons with normal vision.
Reason (R): A son receives his only X chromosome from his mother.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: X-linked recessive inheritance through the mother
solution.explanation: A colour-blind woman has the recessive allele on both X chromosomes. Every son receives one of her X chromosomes and a Y from his father, so all her sons are colour blind, whatever the father's vision. A is false; R is true (and is exactly why A is false).
steps: Mother XᶜXᶜ: every egg carries Xᶜ
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', sex-linked inheritance: colour blindness
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about chromosomal disorders are correct?

(a) An individual with Turner's syndrome is a male with gynaecomastia.
(b) An individual with Klinefelter's syndrome has 44 autosomes and the sex chromosomes XXY, i.e. 47 chromosomes.
(c) Down's syndrome results from polyploidy.
(d) An individual with Turner's syndrome has 44 autosomes and one X chromosome, i.e. 45 chromosomes.
(e) An individual with Down's syndrome has an additional copy of chromosome 21, i.e. 47 chromosomes.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: (a) False: Turner's syndrome individuals are sterile females with rudimentary ovaries; masculine development with gynaecomastia describes Klinefelter's syndrome. (b) True: 44 + XXY = 47. (c) False: Down's syndrome is trisomy 21, an aneuploidy, not polyploidy. (d) True: 44 + X0 = 45. (e) True: 45 autosomes + 2 sex chromosomes = 47.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (a) or (c) include a false statement; '(c) and (e) only' also leaves out (b) and (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', genetic disorders: chromosomal disorders; mutation
solution.final_answer: Option A: (b), (d) and (e) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (result of the test cross AaBb × aabb) with List-II (interpretation).

List-I:
A. Four classes in the ratio 1 : 1 : 1 : 1
B. Only the two parental classes, in the ratio 1 : 1
C. Parental classes 90 per cent, recombinant classes 10 per cent
D. Parental classes 63 per cent, recombinant classes 37 per cent

List-II:
I. Genes on the same chromosome, loosely linked
II. Genes assort independently
III. Genes so tightly linked that no recombination occurs
IV. Genes on the same chromosome, tightly linked

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Independent genes give the four test-cross classes in equal proportion. With no recombination, only the two parental combinations appear. Morgan found that tightly linked genes show very low recombination and loosely linked genes show higher recombination (e.g. 1.3 per cent between yellow body and white eye, 37.2 per cent between white eye and miniature wing in Drosophila).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes confuse independent assortment with complete linkage, or tight with loose linkage.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', linkage and recombination
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A man with blood group AB cannot be the biological father of a child with blood group O.
Statement II: Two parents who both have blood group B can have a child with blood group A.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: A child with blood group O is ii and must receive i from each parent; an AB (IᴬIᴮ) man has no i, so Statement I is true. Parents with blood group B are IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi; neither can pass on Iᴬ, so their children can only be B or O. Statement II is false.
steps: O child needs i from both parents → I true
B × B parents have no Iᴬ → II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', deviations from Mendelism: co-dominance
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, the genetic code is nearly universal; for example, from bacteria to humans UUU codes for phenylalanine. Exceptions to this rule have been found in:

options.text: Chloroplast codons of all green plants

solution.explanation: NCERT lists 'nearly universal' among the features of the genetic code: UUU codes for phenylalanine from bacteria to humans, and some exceptions to this rule have been found in mitochondrial codons and in some protozoans.
solution.why_others_wrong: Bacteria and human nuclear genes follow the standard code (UUU for phenylalanine from bacteria to humans); NCERT does not name chloroplasts as an exception.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', genetic code
solution.final_answer: Option D: Mitochondrial codons and some protozoans

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In a tRNA molecule, the region that has bases complementary to the code (codon) on the mRNA is the:

solution.explanation: NCERT: tRNA has an anticodon loop that has bases complementary to the code, and an amino acid acceptor end to which it binds amino acids. Each amino acid has a specific tRNA.
solution.why_others_wrong: The acceptor end carries the amino acid; the cap and poly-A tail are features of processed eukaryotic mRNA, not of tRNA.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', tRNA – the adapter molecule
solution.final_answer: Option B: Anticodon loop

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The end of a polynucleotide chain at which the sugar has a free 3'-OH group is referred to as the 3'-end of the chain.
Statement II: Two nucleotides in a polynucleotide chain are linked to each other through an N-glycosidic linkage.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Polarity and linkages of a polynucleotide
solution.explanation: NCERT: at one end of the polymer the phosphate moiety at the 5'-end of the sugar is free (5'-end), and at the other end the sugar has a free 3'-OH group, which is the 3'-end (Statement I true). Two nucleotides are linked through a 3'-5' phosphodiester linkage; the N-glycosidic linkage joins a nitrogenous base to the pentose sugar within a nucleoside (Statement II false).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', structure of polynucleotide chain
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (term) with List-II (meaning).

List-I:
A. Exon
B. Intron
C. Cistron
D. Capping

List-II:
I. Addition of methyl guanosine triphosphate to the 5'-end of hnRNA
II. Coding sequence that appears in the mature, processed RNA
III. Segment of DNA coding for a polypeptide
IV. Intervening sequence that is removed by splicing

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Exons are the coding or expressed sequences that appear in mature, processed RNA; introns are intervening sequences that do not appear in mature RNA and are removed by splicing. A cistron is a segment of DNA coding for a polypeptide. In capping, an unusual nucleotide, methyl guanosine triphosphate, is added to the 5'-end of hnRNA.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap exon and intron, cistron and capping, or exon and cistron.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', transcription unit and the gene; transcription
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements comparing RNA and DNA are correct?

(a) DNA is chemically less stable than RNA.
(b) In RNA, uracil is found in place of thymine.
(c) RNA is known to be catalytic, and hence reactive.
(d) RNA is preferred over DNA for the storage of genetic information.
(e) The 2'-OH group present at every nucleotide in RNA makes it labile and easily degradable.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Why DNA, and not RNA, is the predominant genetic material
solution.explanation: (b), (c) and (e) are NCERT statements. Because of its 2'-OH group and catalytic reactivity, RNA is less stable; DNA is chemically less reactive and structurally more stable, so (a) is false and DNA is preferred for the storage of genetic information, making (d) false. RNA is better for the transmission and expression of genetic information.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options including (a) or (d) reverse the comparison of stability or of storage.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', the search for genetic material: properties of genetic material (DNA versus RNA)
solution.final_answer: Option B: (b), (c) and (e) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the Hershey–Chase experiment, bacteria infected with bacteriophages that had been grown in a medium containing radioactive phosphorus became radioactive.
Reason (R): The phage DNA, which contains phosphorus, entered the bacteria, whereas the phage protein coat did not.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Phages grown with radioactive phosphorus have radioactive DNA, because DNA contains phosphorus and protein does not. NCERT: bacteria infected with viruses that had radioactive DNA were radioactive, indicating that DNA was the material that passed from the virus to the bacteria. R gives the reason the bacteria became radioactive.
steps: DNA entered the bacteria → bacteria radioactive
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', the search for genetic material: the genetic material is DNA
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.subtopic: Human genome project and DNA fingerprinting
questions.question_text: NCERT notes that the sensitivity of DNA fingerprinting has been increased by the use of the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). As a consequence:

options.text: Satellite DNA probes are no longer required
Only blood samples can now be used
The DNA of monozygotic twins can now be told apart
DNA from a single cell is enough to perform DNA fingerprinting analysis

solution.explanation: NCERT: the sensitivity of the technique has been increased by the use of PCR; consequently, DNA from a single cell is enough to perform DNA fingerprinting analysis.
steps: A single cell's DNA is enough
solution.why_others_wrong: Labelled VNTR (satellite DNA) probes are still used; DNA from any tissue (blood, hair follicle, skin, bone, saliva, sperm) can be used; identical twins still give the same pattern.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', DNA fingerprinting
solution.final_answer: Option D: DNA from a single cell is enough to perform DNA fingerprinting analysis

questions.subject: Botany
questions.subtopic: Human genome project and DNA fingerprinting
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, which human chromosome was the last of the 24 human chromosomes (22 autosomes, X and Y) to be completely sequenced, in May 2006?

solution.concept: Completion of the human genome sequence
solution.explanation: NCERT: the sequence of chromosome 1 was completed only in May 2006; this was the last of the 24 human chromosomes (22 autosomes and X and Y) to be sequenced. Chromosome 1 is also the chromosome with the most genes (2968).
solution.why_others_wrong: NCERT names chromosome 1, not the Y, 21 or X chromosome, as the last to be sequenced.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', human genome project
solution.final_answer: Option B: Chromosome 1

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A linear double-stranded DNA molecule has 100 base pairs. How many 3'–5' phosphodiester linkages join the nucleotides of its two strands in all?

solution.explanation: In a polynucleotide chain, nucleotides are linked through 3'-5' phosphodiester linkages, one between each pair of neighbouring nucleotides. A linear strand of 100 nucleotides has 99 such linkages, and the two strands together have 2 × 99 = 198.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 assumes one linkage per nucleotide (as in a closed circle); 99 counts only one strand; 400 counts two linkages per nucleotide.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', structure of polynucleotide chain
solution.final_answer: Option D: 198

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: The coding strand of a short stretch of a gene reads 5'-ATGGCATTC-3', and translation starts at the first codon. What is the anticodon of the tRNA that pairs with the second codon of the mRNA, written in the 5'→3' direction?

solution.explanation: The mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand, with U for T: 5'-AUG GCA UUC-3'. The second codon is 5'-GCA-3'. The anticodon pairs with it in antiparallel fashion: 3'-CGU-5', which written 5'→3' is 5'-UGC-3'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5'-CGU-3' writes the anticodon in the wrong direction; 5'-GCA-3' copies the codon itself; 5'-TGC-3' uses thymine, which RNA does not contain.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', transcription; tRNA – the adapter molecule
solution.final_answer: Option D: 5'-UGC-3'

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In the middle of the coding region of an mRNA, a point mutation changes one codon into UAG. What is the most likely effect on the polypeptide?

options.text: Translation stops at this codon, giving a shorter polypeptide, because UAG is a stop codon at which a release factor binds
The reading frame shifts, so every amino acid after this point is changed
UAG is read by its own specific tRNA, so the polypeptide is unchanged
The polypeptide becomes longer, because translation continues past the normal stop codon

solution.explanation: UAG is one of the three codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) that do not code for any amino acid and act as stop codons. At the end of translation, a release factor binds to the stop codon, terminating translation and releasing the polypeptide. A stop codon created in the middle of the message therefore ends the polypeptide early.
solution.why_others_wrong: A substitution does not shift the reading frame (that needs an insertion or deletion); stop codons have no tRNA; an early stop shortens rather than lengthens the polypeptide.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', genetic code; translation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Translation stops at this codon, giving a shorter polypeptide, because UAG is a stop codon at which a release factor binds

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Histones are positively charged proteins.
Reason (R): Histones are rich in the basic amino acid residues lysine and arginine, which carry positive charges in their side chains.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: in eukaryotes there is a set of positively charged, basic proteins called histones. A protein acquires charge depending on the abundance of amino acid residues with charged side chains; histones are rich in lysine and arginine, both of which carry positive charges in their side chains. R therefore explains A.
steps: Positive side chains of lysine and arginine make histones positive
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', packaging of DNA helix
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Griffith concluded that the R strain bacteria had somehow been transformed by the heat-killed S strain bacteria, through some 'transforming principle'.
Statement II: Griffith identified this transforming principle as DNA.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: From transformation to its biochemical basis
solution.explanation: NCERT: Griffith concluded that the R strain bacteria had somehow been transformed by the heat-killed S strain bacteria; some 'transforming principle' transferred from the heat-killed S strain enabled the R strain to make a smooth polysaccharide coat (Statement I true). However, the biochemical nature of the genetic material was not defined from his experiments; Avery, MacLeod and McCarty later worked out that it was DNA (Statement II false).
steps: Biochemical nature identified later by Avery, MacLeod and McCarty
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', the search for genetic material: transforming principle
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (experiment) with List-II (observation).

List-I:
A. Meselson and Stahl: E. coli from ¹⁵N medium grown for one generation (20 minutes) in ¹⁴N medium
B. Hershey and Chase: bacteria infected with phages grown in radioactive sulphur
C. Avery, MacLeod and McCarty: transforming extract treated with DNase
D. Griffith: mice injected with heat-killed S strain bacteria alone

List-II:
I. The mice lived
II. Transformation of R strain bacteria was inhibited
III. The bacterial cells were not radioactive
IV. The DNA had a hybrid (intermediate) density

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Classic experiments on the genetic material
solution.explanation: After one generation in ¹⁴N, all the DNA was of hybrid density (semiconservative replication). Bacteria infected with phages carrying radioactive (sulphur-labelled) protein were not radioactive, since the protein did not enter. DNase inhibited transformation, showing the transforming principle was DNA. Heat-killed S strain bacteria alone did not kill the mice.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the Meselson–Stahl and Hershey–Chase results, the Avery and Griffith results, or the Hershey–Chase and Avery results.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', the search for genetic material; replication: the experimental proof
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the processing of RNA in eukaryotes are correct?

(a) The precursor of mRNA, the heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA), is transcribed by RNA polymerase II.
(b) In capping, an unusual nucleotide (methyl guanosine triphosphate) is added to the 5'-end of hnRNA.
(c) In tailing, adenylate residues are added at the 3'-end in a template-dependent manner.
(d) In splicing, the introns are removed and the exons are joined in a defined order.
(e) The fully processed hnRNA, now called mRNA, is translated inside the nucleus.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: (a), (b) and (d) are NCERT statements. (c) is false: in tailing, adenylate residues (200–300) are added at the 3'-end in a template-independent manner. (e) is false: the fully processed hnRNA, now called mRNA, is transported out of the nucleus for translation.
steps: (e): mRNA is transported to the cytoplasm
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (c) or (e) include a false statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', transcription: transcription in eukaryotes
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: E. coli grown for many generations in a ¹⁴NH₄Cl medium is transferred to a ¹⁵NH₄Cl medium and allowed to divide twice (40 minutes; generation time 20 minutes). If replication is semiconservative, the DNA extracted after 40 minutes will be:

solution.explanation: Each new DNA molecule keeps one parental strand and gets one new strand. After the first division in ¹⁵N, both molecules are ¹⁴N/¹⁵N (hybrid). In the second division, each hybrid gives one ¹⁴N/¹⁵N and one ¹⁵N/¹⁵N molecule. So after 40 minutes: 2 hybrid and 2 heavy out of 4, i.e. half and half. (This mirrors Meselson and Stahl's result of equal light and hybrid DNA after 40 minutes, with the isotopes reversed.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Half hybrid and half light' is the result for the original direction (¹⁵N → ¹⁴N); 'all hybrid' is the result after one generation; three-fourths heavy would be the result after three generations.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', replication: the experimental proof
solution.final_answer: Option B: Half hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N) and half heavy (¹⁵N/¹⁵N)

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which sequence correctly shows increasing levels of DNA packaging in a eukaryotic nucleus, as described in NCERT?

options.text: Chromatin fibres → nucleosome → 'beads-on-string' chromatin → condensed chromosome at metaphase
Nucleosome → condensed chromosome at metaphase → chromatin fibres → 'beads-on-string' chromatin
DNA wrapped around a histone octamer (nucleosome) → 'beads-on-string' chromatin → chromatin fibres → condensed chromosome at metaphase
'Beads-on-string' chromatin → nucleosome → chromatin fibres → condensed chromosome at metaphase

solution.explanation: NCERT: the negatively charged DNA is wrapped around the positively charged histone octamer to form a nucleosome. Nucleosomes are the repeating units of chromatin, which looks like 'beads-on-string' under the electron microscope. The beads-on-string structure is packaged into chromatin fibres, which are further coiled and condensed at metaphase to form chromosomes.
solution.why_others_wrong: In the other sequences a higher level of packaging is placed before the nucleosome, or the beads-on-string stage (a chain of nucleosomes) is placed before the nucleosome itself.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', packaging of DNA helix
solution.final_answer: Option C: DNA wrapped around a histone octamer (nucleosome) → 'beads-on-string' chromatin → chromatin fibres → condensed chromosome at metaphase

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A mutant E. coli makes a lac repressor that still binds normally to the operator but can no longer interact with the inducer. The mutant is placed in a medium containing lactose and no glucose. What happens to the lac operon?

options.text: It is switched on, because lactose binds directly to the operator and displaces the repressor
It is switched on, because permease brings lactose into the cell
It is expressed all the time, whether or not lactose is present
It remains switched off, because the repressor cannot be inactivated by the inducer and stays bound to the operator

solution.explanation: NCERT: the repressor, synthesised all the time from the i gene, binds to the operator and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon. In the presence of an inducer such as lactose or allolactose, the repressor is inactivated by interaction with the inducer, allowing RNA polymerase access to the promoter. If the repressor cannot interact with the inducer, it is never inactivated, stays on the operator, and the z, y and a genes are not transcribed even when lactose is available.
steps: No interaction → repressor stays on the operator
solution.why_others_wrong: The inducer acts on the repressor, not on the operator; lactose entry alone cannot switch the operon on if the repressor is not inactivated; constitutive expression would need a repressor that cannot bind the operator, the opposite of this mutant.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', regulation of gene expression: the lac operon
solution.final_answer: Option D: It remains switched off, because the repressor cannot be inactivated by the inducer and stays bound to the operator

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A eukaryotic structural gene has three exons of 150, 120 and 90 nucleotides, separated by two introns of 180 and 60 nucleotides. Assume the exons contain no untranslated regions: the start codon AUG begins the first exon and a stop codon ends the third exon. How many amino acids will the polypeptide translated from the mature mRNA have (before any processing)?

solution.explanation: Splicing removes the introns, so the mature mRNA carries only the exons: 150 + 120 + 90 = 360 nucleotides = 120 codons. The last codon is a stop codon, which does not code for any amino acid, so the polypeptide has 120 − 1 = 119 amino acids.
steps: Minus the stop codon: 119 amino acids
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 counts the stop codon as an amino acid; 199 and 200 wrongly keep the 240 intron nucleotides in the mRNA (600 nucleotides).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', transcription: split genes and splicing; genetic code
solution.final_answer: Option B: 119

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Deletion of a single base near the beginning of the coding region of a gene changes the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide from that point onwards.
Reason (R): The genetic code is degenerate: some amino acids are coded by more than one codon.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: insertion or deletion of one or two bases changes the reading frame from the point of insertion or deletion (A true). This happens because the codon is a triplet read in a contiguous fashion without punctuation. Degeneracy (R) is a true feature of the code, but it concerns how many codons specify an amino acid and has nothing to do with the shift of the reading frame.
steps: Cause of A: triplet code read without punctuation, not degeneracy
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', genetic code: mutations and genetic code
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements comparing gene expression in bacteria and eukaryotes are correct?

(a) In bacteria, a single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyses the transcription of all types of RNA.
(b) Bacterial structural genes are mostly monocistronic.
(c) In bacteria, translation can begin much before the mRNA is fully transcribed.
(d) In eukaryotes, the primary transcript is functional without any processing.
(e) In eukaryotes, the structural genes are split, with exons interrupted by introns.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: (a) True. (b) False: the structural gene in a transcription unit is mostly monocistronic in eukaryotes and polycistronic in bacteria. (c) True: bacterial mRNA needs no processing and there is no nuclear separation, so transcription and translation can be coupled. (d) False: the eukaryotic primary transcript contains introns and is non-functional until it is processed by capping, tailing and splicing. (e) True.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (b) or (d) include a false statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', transcription unit and the gene; transcription
solution.final_answer: Option A: (a), (c) and (e) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (quantity for a B-DNA double helix of 500 base pairs in which 20 per cent of all the bases are adenine) with List-II (value).

List-I:
A. Number of adenine bases
B. Number of guanine bases
C. Number of hydrogen bonds between the two strands (A=T two, G≡C three)
D. Number of complete turns of the helix (about 10 base pairs per turn)

List-II:
I. 50
II. 300
III. 1300
IV. 200

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Chargaff's rule and the dimensions of B-DNA
solution.explanation: 500 bp = 1000 bases. A = 20% of 1000 = 200, and A = T, so T = 200. G + C = 600 and G = C, so G = 300. Hydrogen bonds = 2 × 200 (A=T pairs) + 3 × 300 (G≡C pairs) = 1300. The pitch is 3.4 nm and the rise per base pair 0.34 nm, so there are about 10 bp per turn: 500/10 = 50 turns.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the adenine and guanine counts, the turns and hydrogen bonds, or the guanine and hydrogen-bond values.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', structure of polynucleotide chain
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: If one strand of a DNA double helix has its bases in the ratio A : G : T : C = 1 : 2 : 3 : 4, the complementary strand has A : G : T : C = 3 : 4 : 1 : 2.
Statement II: In the first strand, the ratio (A + G)/(T + C) is equal to one.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Base pairing within and between strands
solution.explanation: Base pairing makes the bases of one strand complementary to those of the other: A of strand 2 = T of strand 1 (3), G of strand 2 = C of strand 1 (4), T of strand 2 = A of strand 1 (1), C of strand 2 = G of strand 1 (2). Statement I is true. Chargaff's equalities (A = T, G = C) hold for double-stranded DNA as a whole, not for a single strand: here (A + G)/(T + C) = (1 + 2)/(3 + 4) = 3/7. Statement II is false.
steps: Strand 2: A 3, G 4, T 1, C 2 → I true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', structure of polynucleotide chain: Chargaff's rules
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In Griffith's experiments with Streptococcus pneumoniae, what would be expected if mice were injected with a mixture of heat-killed R strain bacteria and live S strain bacteria?

options.text: The mice would die, because the live S strain bacteria are virulent on their own
The mice would live, because the heat-killed R strain transforms the S strain into the R form
The mice would live, because heat-killed bacteria protect the mice from infection
The mice would die only if the mixture were first treated with DNase

solution.explanation: Griffith found that mice injected with live S strain bacteria (which have a mucous polysaccharide coat) died, while those injected with live R strain lived. Transformation in his experiment converted harmless R into virulent S using the transforming principle from heat-killed S. In the mixture here, live S bacteria are already present and virulent, so the mice die whatever the heat-killed R bacteria do.
steps: Live S strain alone kills mice
Heat-killed R cannot remove the coat of live S
solution.why_others_wrong: Griffith's transformation turned R into S, not S into R; heat-killed bacteria give no protection in his experiments; DNase destroys DNA and is irrelevant when live S bacteria are injected.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', the search for genetic material: transforming principle
solution.final_answer: Option A: The mice would die, because the live S strain bacteria are virulent on their own

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria serve as important biofertilisers in paddy fields. Besides fixing atmospheric nitrogen, NCERT notes that they also:

options.text: Absorb phosphorus from the soil and pass it to the rice plants
Kill the caterpillars that feed on the rice plants
Add organic matter to the soil and increase its fertility
Release antibiotics that kill the weeds of paddy fields

solution.explanation: NCERT: cyanobacteria are autotrophic microbes widely distributed in aquatic and terrestrial environments, many of which can fix atmospheric nitrogen; in paddy fields they serve as an important biofertiliser. Blue-green algae also add organic matter to the soil and increase its fertility.
steps: Also add organic matter → greater soil fertility
solution.why_others_wrong: Absorbing phosphorus for the plant is the role of mycorrhizal fungi such as Glomus; killing caterpillars is the role of Bacillus thuringiensis; weed killing by antibiotics is not described in NCERT.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', microbes as biofertilisers
solution.final_answer: Option C: Add organic matter to the soil and increase its fertility

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (need) with List-II (microbial product used).

List-I:
A. Suppressing the immune response of an organ-transplant patient
B. Removing a clot from the blood vessels of a patient with myocardial infarction
C. Lowering blood cholesterol
D. Removing oily stains from laundry

List-II:
I. Lipases
II. Statins
III. Cyclosporin A
IV. Streptokinase

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Bioactive molecules and enzymes from microbes
solution.explanation: Cyclosporin A, from the fungus Trichoderma polysporum, is used as an immunosuppressive agent in organ-transplant patients. Streptokinase, produced by Streptococcus and modified by genetic engineering, is a 'clot buster' for patients with myocardial infarction. Statins from Monascus purpureus are blood-cholesterol lowering agents. Lipases are used in detergent formulations to remove oily stains from laundry.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap cyclosporin A with streptokinase, lipases with statins, or cyclosporin A with statins.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', microbes in industrial products: enzymes and other bioactive molecules
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which gas does NCERT list among the gases produced in the anaerobic sludge digesters of a sewage treatment plant, but not among the gases produced by methanogens growing anaerobically on cellulosic material?

solution.concept: Comparing two NCERT lists of gases
solution.explanation: NCERT: certain bacteria that grow anaerobically on cellulosic material produce large amounts of methane along with CO₂ and H₂ (methanogens). In the anaerobic sludge digesters, bacteria produce a mixture of gases such as methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide, which form biogas. Hydrogen sulphide appears only in the second list; hydrogen appears only in the first.
steps: Methanogens on cellulose: CH₄, CO₂, H₂
Only in the digester list: H₂S
solution.why_others_wrong: Methane and carbon dioxide are in both lists; hydrogen is in the methanogen list only.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', microbes in sewage treatment; microbes in production of biogas
solution.final_answer: Option D: Hydrogen sulphide

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The large holes in 'Swiss cheese' are due to the production of a large amount of CO₂ by the bacterium Propionibacterium sharmanii.
Reason (R): 'Roquefort cheese' is ripened by growing a specific bacterium on it, which gives it a particular flavour.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: the large holes in Swiss cheese are due to the production of a large amount of CO₂ by a bacterium named Propionibacterium sharmanii (A true). 'Roquefort cheese' is ripened by growing a specific fungus on it, not a bacterium, which gives it a particular flavour (R false).
steps: Roquefort cheese: ripened by a fungus
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', microbes in household products
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about municipal sewage treatment are correct?

(a) In primary treatment, floating debris is removed by sequential filtration, and grit is removed by sedimentation.
(b) The primary sludge, rather than the primary effluent, is taken for secondary treatment in the aeration tanks.
(c) In the aeration tanks, the vigorous growth of aerobic microbes into flocs reduces the BOD of the effluent.
(d) A small part of the activated sludge is pumped back into the aeration tank to serve as the inoculum.
(e) The flocs in the aeration tank consist of anaerobic methanogens.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: (a) True. (b) False: all the solids that settle form the primary sludge, and the supernatant forms the primary effluent, which is taken for secondary treatment. (c) True: aerobic microbes grow into flocs (masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments) and consume the organic matter, reducing BOD. (d) True; the major part of the sludge goes to anaerobic sludge digesters. (e) False: flocs form from aerobic microbes in the aerated tank.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (b) or (e) include a false statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', microbes in sewage treatment
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Alexander Fleming, while working on Staphylococci bacteria, observed a mould growing in one of his unwashed culture plates, around which the Staphylococci could not grow.
Statement II: The fungus Trichoderma polysporum is the source of cyclosporin A, and Trichoderma species are also used as biological control agents against several plant pathogens.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Fungi as sources of drugs and as biocontrol agents
solution.explanation: NCERT: Fleming, while working on Staphylococci, once observed a mould growing in one of his unwashed culture plates around which Staphylococci could not grow; the chemical was penicillin, from Penicillium notatum (Statement I true). Cyclosporin A, an immunosuppressive agent, is produced by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum, and Trichoderma species, free-living fungi common in root ecosystems, are effective biocontrol agents of several plant pathogens (Statement II true).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', antibiotics; bioactive molecules; microbes as biocontrol agents
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about methanogens are correct?

(a) They grow anaerobically on cellulosic material.
(b) They are commonly found in the anaerobic sludge during sewage treatment.
(c) They are present in the rumen of cattle, where they help in the breakdown of cellulose.
(d) The excreta (dung) of cattle, commonly called gobar, is rich in these bacteria.
(e) The gas they produce is mainly hydrogen.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Methanogens in nature and in biogas plants
solution.explanation: NCERT: bacteria that grow anaerobically on cellulosic material produce large amounts of methane along with CO₂ and H₂; they are collectively called methanogens, e.g. Methanobacterium. They are commonly found in the anaerobic sludge during sewage treatment and in the rumen of cattle, where they help break down cellulose; cattle dung (gobar) is rich in them and is used to make biogas. The gas they produce is mainly methane, so (e) is false.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (e) include a false statement; '(a), (c) and (d) only' leaves out the true (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', microbes in production of biogas
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: NCERT notes that totally unrelated species can also compete for the same resource. In some shallow South American lakes, visiting flamingoes and resident fishes compete for their common food, which is the:

solution.explanation: NCERT: competition is thought to occur when closely related species compete for the same resources that are limiting, but totally unrelated species could also compete; in some shallow South American lakes, visiting flamingoes and resident fishes compete for their common food, the zooplankton in the lake.
steps: Flamingoes and fishes: common food = zooplankton
solution.why_others_wrong: NCERT names zooplankton as the shared food; phytoplankton, insect larvae and snails are not mentioned.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions: competition
solution.final_answer: Option B: Zooplankton in the lake

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Consider the six population interactions described in NCERT: mutualism, competition, predation, parasitism, commensalism and amensalism. In how many of them does at least one of the two interacting species benefit?

solution.explanation: Mutualism (+, +), predation (+, −), parasitism (+, −) and commensalism (+, 0) each have at least one species that benefits. In competition (−, −) both lose, and in amensalism (−, 0) one is harmed and the other unaffected, so neither of these benefits any species. Count = 4.
steps: Benefit present: mutualism, predation, parasitism, commensalism
solution.why_others_wrong: Two counts only the interactions in which one benefits and one is harmed; three leaves out mutualism or commensalism; five wrongly includes amensalism or competition.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions
solution.final_answer: Option D: Four

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (example) with List-II (interaction).

List-I:
A. A sparrow eating seeds
B. A koel (cuckoo) laying its eggs in a crow's nest
C. The fig and its pollinating wasp
D. Introduced goats and the Abingdon tortoise of the Galapagos

List-II:
I. Competition
II. Mutualism
III. Predation
IV. Brood parasitism

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: a sparrow eating any seed is no less a predator than a tiger eating a deer. The cuckoo (koel) lays its eggs in the nest of its host, the crow, which incubates them (brood parasitism). The fig and its wasp are mutualists: the wasp pollinates the fig and uses its fruit for egg-laying. The Abingdon tortoise became extinct within a decade of goats being introduced, apparently because the goats were better browsers (competition).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap predation with brood parasitism, mutualism with competition, or predation with mutualism.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In logistic growth, the population density eventually reaches an asymptote when it reaches the carrying capacity (K) of the habitat.
Statement II: In nature, a given habitat has enough resources to support an unlimited number of individuals.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: in nature, a given habitat has enough resources to support a maximum possible number, beyond which no further growth is possible; this limit is the carrying capacity (K). A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows lag, acceleration and deceleration phases and finally an asymptote at K (Statement I true). Resources are not unlimited (Statement II false).
steps: Statement II: false (resources are limited; K exists)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population: population growth models
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In a population of 1000 individuals, 600 are pre-reproductive, 300 are reproductive and 100 are post-reproductive. What percentage of the population is pre-reproductive, and what does the age pyramid of this population indicate?

solution.concept: Age distribution and the age pyramid
solution.explanation: Pre-reproductive share = 600/1000 = 60 per cent. Plotting the per cent of individuals in each age group gives an age pyramid; here the pre-reproductive base is the broadest and each older group is narrower, giving a triangular pyramid, which NCERT associates with an expanding (growing) population. A bell shape indicates a stable population and an urn shape a declining one.
solution.why_others_wrong: The broad base is not the bell shape of a stable population; 30 per cent is the reproductive share; 40 per cent is the share that is not pre-reproductive.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population attributes: age pyramids
solution.final_answer: Option A: 60 per cent; an expanding (growing) population

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: On the rocky sea coasts of Scotland, the larger and competitively superior barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller barnacle Chthamalus from that zone. If Balanus were experimentally removed from the area, what would be expected?

options.text: Chthamalus would decline, because it depends on Balanus for food
Chthamalus would expand its distribution into that zone, an example of competitive release
Both barnacles would decline, because the interaction is mutualism
There would be no change, because barnacles do not compete for space

solution.explanation: NCERT cites Connell's field experiments: on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland, the larger and competitively superior barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller barnacle Chthamalus from that zone. It also explains competitive release: a species whose distribution is restricted to a small area because of a competitively superior species expands its range dramatically when the competing species is removed.
solution.why_others_wrong: The barnacles compete; Chthamalus does not depend on Balanus, the interaction is not mutualism, and competition for space is exactly what restricts Chthamalus.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions: competition
solution.final_answer: Option B: Chthamalus would expand its distribution into that zone, an example of competitive release

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Predators help in maintaining species diversity in a community.
Reason (R): Predators reduce the intensity of competition among competing prey species.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: predators also help in maintaining species diversity in a community, by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species. Without them, a competitively superior prey species could eliminate others (as in the Pisaster removal experiment). R is the mechanism behind A.
steps: Less competition among prey → more prey species coexist: R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions: predation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about measuring population size are correct according to NCERT?

(a) Total number of individuals is always the most appropriate measure of population density.
(b) Where a single huge banyan tree grows among 200 Parthenium plants, percent cover or biomass is a more meaningful measure of population size than numbers.
(c) Absolute population densities are always required for every ecological investigation.
(d) To know whether the fish population of a lake has changed, the number of fish caught per trap is good enough.
(e) The tiger census in national parks and tiger reserves is often based on pug marks and fecal pellets.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Absolute and relative measures of population density
solution.explanation: (a) False: total number is generally, not always, the most appropriate measure; it is sometimes meaningless or difficult to determine. (b) True. (c) False: for certain investigations absolute numbers are not needed and relative densities serve the purpose. (d) True. (e) True: population density can be estimated indirectly.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (a) or (c) include a false statement; '(b), (c) and (d)' also leaves out (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population attributes
solution.final_answer: Option D: (b), (d) and (e) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (process affecting population density) with List-II (meaning).

List-I:
A. Natality
B. Mortality
C. Immigration
D. Emigration

List-II:
I. Number of individuals of the population who left the habitat and went elsewhere during a given period
II. Number of births during a given period that are added to the initial density
III. Number of individuals of the same species that have come into the habitat from elsewhere during a given period
IV. Number of deaths in the population during a given period

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Four basic processes that change population density
solution.explanation: NCERT: natality is the number of births during a given period added to the initial density; mortality is the number of deaths during a given period; immigration is the number of individuals of the same species that have come into the habitat from elsewhere; emigration is the number of individuals of the population who left the habitat and gone elsewhere. Natality and immigration increase density; mortality and emigration decrease it.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap births with deaths, arrivals with departures, or births with arrivals.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population: population growth
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: NCERT gives the intrinsic rate of natural increase (r) as 0.12 for the flour beetle, 0.015 for the Norway rat and 0.0205 for the human population of India in 1981. If each population grew exponentially at its r (taking the same unit of time for all, and ln 2 = 0.693), which would double in the shortest time and which in the longest?

options.text: Shortest: Norway rat; longest: flour beetle
Shortest: flour beetle; longest: human population of India
Shortest: flour beetle; longest: Norway rat
Shortest: human population of India; longest: Norway rat

solution.explanation: For exponential growth, Nₜ = N₀e^(rt); the population doubles when e^(rt) = 2, i.e. t = ln 2/r = 0.693/r. Flour beetle: 0.693/0.12 ≈ 5.8; human (India): 0.693/0.0205 ≈ 33.8; Norway rat: 0.693/0.015 ≈ 46.2 time units. The larger the r, the shorter the doubling time.
solution.shortcut: Doubling time is inversely proportional to r: largest r doubles fastest, smallest r slowest.
solution.why_others_wrong: The first option reverses the relation between r and doubling time; the human population (r = 0.0205) doubles faster than the Norway rat (r = 0.015), so it is neither the slowest nor the fastest.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population growth: exponential growth
solution.final_answer: Option C: Shortest: flour beetle; longest: Norway rat

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The Abingdon tortoise in the Galapagos Islands became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced on the island.
Reason (R): The introduced goats had a greater browsing efficiency than the tortoise.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT gives this as an example of competition: the Abingdon tortoise became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced on the island, apparently due to the greater browsing efficiency of the goats. The goats' superior efficiency in using the shared food (R) is the stated reason for the tortoise's extinction (A).
steps: Superior competitor for the same food eliminated the tortoise: R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions: competition
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In interference competition, the feeding efficiency of one species may be reduced by the interfering and inhibitory presence of the other species, even if resources (food and space) are abundant.
Statement II: According to Gause's competitive exclusion principle, two closely related species competing for the same resources can co-exist indefinitely if they are equally abundant.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: in interspecific competition the feeding efficiency of one species might be reduced due to the interfering and inhibitory presence of the other species, even if resources are abundant (Statement I true). Gause's principle states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely, and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually (Statement II false).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions: competition
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about parasitism are correct?

(a) The life cycles of endoparasites are simpler than those of ectoparasites.
(b) Parasites might render the host more vulnerable to predation by making it physically weak.
(c) The eggs of a brood-parasitic bird have evolved to resemble the host's eggs in size and colour.
(d) Parasites always kill their hosts quickly.
(e) Many parasites have evolved to be host-specific, so that the host and the parasite tend to co-evolve.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: (a) False: the life cycles of endoparasites are more complex because of their extreme specialisation. (b) True. (c) True: this reduces the chances of the host bird detecting and ejecting the foreign eggs. (d) False: parasites may reduce the survival, growth and reproduction of the host and reduce its population density; NCERT does not say they always kill quickly. (e) True.
steps: (a): endoparasite life cycles are more complex
(d): parasites harm, not necessarily kill quickly
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (a) or (d) include a false statement; '(b), (c) and (d)' also leaves out (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions: parasitism
solution.final_answer: Option A: (b), (c) and (e) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the processes of decomposition described in NCERT?
