A child is born without functional B-lymphocytes, but his T-lymphocytes are normal. Which of the following are expected?

(a) Vaccination with weakened pathogens will produce high levels of antibodies.
(b) The humoral immune response fails, since antibodies are not produced.
(c) Cell-mediated immunity, such as rejection of a mismatched graft, can still occur.
(d) Passive immunity can still be provided by injecting preformed antibodies.
(e) Innate barriers such as the skin, stomach acid and phagocytes are also absent.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: B-cells, T-cells and kinds of immunity
solution.explanation: NCERT: B-lymphocytes produce antibodies (humoral immune response); T-lymphocytes mediate cell-mediated immunity (CMI), which is responsible for graft rejection, and T-cells do not secrete antibodies. Passive immunity uses ready-made antibodies given from outside. Innate immunity (physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine barriers) is non-specific and does not depend on B-cells.
steps: (a) false - no B-cells, so no antibodies even after vaccination
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) needs B-cells to make antibodies, and (e) wrongly ties innate barriers to B-cells; options containing either are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 7 'Human Health and Disease', Immunity
solution.final_answer: Option A: (b), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: In a patient the bone marrow stops functioning, but the thymus is normal. Based on NCERT's account of the lymphoid organs, what is expected?

options.text: Only B-lymphocytes fall; T-lymphocytes continue to be produced by the thymus itself
Lymphocytes are unaffected, since they are produced in the lymph nodes
The supply of both B- and T-lymphocytes falls, because all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are produced in the bone marrow
Only red blood cells fall, since lymphocytes are not blood cells

solution.explanation: NCERT: the bone marrow is the main lymphoid organ where all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are produced. The thymus provides the micro-environment for the development and maturation of T-lymphocytes but does not produce lymphocytes from nothing. If the marrow fails, the supply of both B- and T-lymphocytes falls.
steps: All blood cells, including lymphocytes, come from the bone marrow
Thymus only matures T-cells that come to it
Marrow failure -> both B- and T-lymphocytes fall
solution.why_others_wrong: The thymus matures, but does not produce, lymphocytes; lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs where lymphocytes meet antigens; and lymphocytes are blood cells made in the marrow.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 7 'Human Health and Disease', Immunity (Lymphoid organs)
solution.final_answer: Option C: The supply of both B- and T-lymphocytes falls, because all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are produced in the bone marrow

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Heroin is a depressant and slows down body functions.
Reason (R): Heroin is obtained by the methylation of morphine.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: heroin, commonly called smack, is chemically diacetylmorphine, a white, odourless, bitter crystalline compound obtained by ACETYLATION of morphine, which is extracted from the latex of the poppy plant. Heroin is a depressant and slows down body functions. A is true; R names the wrong reaction.
solution.why_others_wrong: R is false, so the two 'both true' options are wrong; A is true, so 'A false but R true' is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 7 'Human Health and Disease', Drugs and Alcohol Abuse
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (pathogen) with List-II (how it reaches a healthy person).

List-I:
A. Ascaris
B. Entamoeba histolytica
C. Streptococcus pneumoniae
D. Plasmodium

List-II:
I. By inhaling droplets or aerosols released by an infected person, or by sharing glasses and utensils
II. As eggs taken in with water, vegetables or fruits contaminated by the faeces of an infected person
III. Through drinking water and food contaminated by faecal matter, with houseflies carrying the parasite to the food
IV. As sporozoites injected by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: eggs of Ascaris are excreted with the faeces of infected persons and contaminate soil, water and plants; a healthy person acquires the infection through contaminated water, vegetables, fruits, etc. For amoebiasis, houseflies act as mechanical carriers that transmit the parasite from faeces to food, and drinking water and food contaminated by faecal matter are the main source of infection. Pneumonia is acquired by inhaling droplets/aerosols released by an infected person or by sharing glasses and utensils. Plasmodium enters as sporozoites through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.
solution.why_others_wrong: Ascaris and Entamoeba both spread by faecal contamination, but only Ascaris is described as taken in as eggs and only amoebiasis with houseflies as carriers; pneumonia is air-borne and malaria vector-borne.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 7 'Human Health and Disease', Common Diseases in Humans
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (component of HIV infection) with List-II (description in NCERT).

List-I:
A. Macrophages
B. Helper T-lymphocytes
C. Reverse transcriptase
D. ELISA

List-II:
I. A widely used diagnostic test for AIDS
II. Enzyme with whose help the viral RNA genome is replicated to form viral DNA
III. Their number decreases progressively in the infected person
IV. Continue to produce virus particles and act like an HIV factory

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: after entering the body, HIV enters macrophages, where its RNA genome is replicated to form viral DNA with the help of reverse transcriptase; the viral DNA is incorporated into the host DNA and the infected cells produce virus particles, so macrophages act like an HIV factory. HIV also enters helper T-lymphocytes, whose number decreases progressively. A widely used diagnostic test for AIDS is ELISA.
solution.why_others_wrong: The commonest trap swaps macrophages and helper T-cells: macrophages keep producing virus, while it is the helper T-cell count that falls. The other codes confuse the enzyme with the test.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 7 'Human Health and Disease', AIDS
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Avoiding stagnation of water around houses and regularly cleaning household coolers helps to control both dengue and chikungunya.
Statement II: Introducing fishes like Gambusia into ponds can also help control filariasis, since the fishes feed on mosquito larvae.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: the vectors of dengue and chikungunya are Aedes mosquitoes; measures such as avoiding stagnation of water near residential areas and regular cleaning of household coolers control mosquito breeding. Gambusia feeds on mosquito larvae, and filarial worms are transmitted through the bite of female mosquito vectors, so reducing mosquitoes also helps control filariasis.
steps: Statement I: true - both diseases spread by Aedes; breeding sites removed
Statement II: true - filariasis is mosquito-borne; Gambusia eats mosquito larvae
solution.why_others_wrong: Both measures reduce mosquito vectors, and NCERT names mosquitoes as the vectors of dengue, chikungunya and filariasis, so neither statement is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 7 'Human Health and Disease', Common Diseases in Humans
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
A man has smoked and chewed tobacco for many years. According to NCERT, he is at increased risk of which of the following?

(a) Cancer of the lung
(b) Cancer of the oral cavity
(c) Bronchitis and emphysema
(d) Coronary heart disease
(e) An increase in the concentration of haem-bound oxygen in his blood

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: smoking is associated with increased incidence of cancers of the lung, urinary bladder and throat, bronchitis, emphysema, coronary heart disease, gastric ulcer, etc.; tobacco chewing is associated with increased risk of cancer of the oral cavity. Smoking increases the carbon monoxide content of blood and REDUCES the concentration of haem-bound oxygen, causing oxygen deficiency in the body.
steps: (e) false - haem-bound oxygen is reduced by CO
solution.why_others_wrong: Smoking raises carbon monoxide and lowers haem-bound oxygen, so (e) is the reverse of NCERT; every option with (e) is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 7 'Human Health and Disease', Drugs and Alcohol Abuse
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Small-volume cultures cannot yield appreciable quantities of products. According to NCERT, bioreactors are used for large-scale production because in them large volumes of culture can be processed, of about:

solution.explanation: NCERT: to produce in large quantities, bioreactors are developed where large volumes (100-1000 litres) of culture can be processed. Bioreactors can be thought of as vessels in which raw materials are biologically converted into specific products.
solution.why_others_wrong: Millilitre and sub-litre volumes are small laboratory cultures, which NCERT says cannot give appreciable yields; millions of litres is far beyond NCERT's figure.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Obtaining the foreign gene product)
solution.final_answer: Option B: 100 to 1000 litres

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: The discovery of which enzymes, often called 'molecular scissors', made it possible to cut DNA at specific locations and thus to construct the first recombinant DNA?

solution.explanation: NCERT: the cutting of DNA at specific locations became possible with the discovery of the so-called 'molecular scissors' - restriction enzymes. The cut piece of DNA was then linked with the plasmid DNA by the enzyme DNA ligase.
steps: Cutting at specific sites -> restriction enzymes (molecular scissors)
solution.why_others_wrong: DNA ligase joins DNA fragments rather than cutting them; DNA polymerase synthesises DNA; ribonuclease removes RNA during DNA isolation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Principles of Biotechnology
solution.final_answer: Option D: Restriction enzymes

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, more than 900 restriction enzymes are known today, each recognising a different recognition sequence. These enzymes have been isolated from:

options.text: A single strain of Escherichia coli

solution.explanation: NCERT: today we know more than 900 restriction enzymes that have been isolated from over 230 strains of bacteria, each of which recognises different recognition sequences.
solution.why_others_wrong: Restriction enzymes are bacterial enzymes that restrict phage growth; they come from many bacterial strains, not one strain of E. coli, and not from fungi or from the phages themselves.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Restriction enzymes)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Over 230 strains of bacteria

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (part of a stirred-tank bioreactor) with List-II (function).

List-I:
A. Stirrer (agitator)
B. Sparger
C. Sampling ports
D. Foam control system

List-II:
I. Controls the foam formed in the culture
II. Allows small volumes of the culture to be withdrawn periodically
III. Bubbles sterile air through the culture, greatly increasing the area for oxygen transfer
IV. Facilitates even mixing and oxygen availability throughout the bioreactor

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: the stirrer facilitates even mixing and oxygen availability throughout the bioreactor; in sparged stirred-tank bioreactors sterile air bubbles are sparged, which greatly increases the area for oxygen transfer; a bioreactor has an agitator system, an oxygen delivery system, a foam control system, a temperature control system, a pH control system and sampling ports so that small volumes of the culture can be withdrawn periodically.
solution.why_others_wrong: Both the stirrer and the sparger help oxygen supply, but only the sparger bubbles air; sampling ports remove small samples and do not add medium.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Obtaining the foreign gene product)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): DNA fragments separated by agarose gel electrophoresis are seen as bright orange-coloured bands after staining with ethidium bromide and exposure to UV radiation.
Reason (R): Ethidium bromide cuts DNA into smaller fragments of different sizes.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: the separated DNA fragments can be visualised only after staining the DNA with a compound known as ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation; the DNA fragments are seen as bright orange coloured bands. Ethidium bromide is a stain; DNA is cut by restriction enzymes before electrophoresis. A is true, R false.
steps: R: false - restriction enzymes cut DNA; ethidium bromide only stains it
solution.why_others_wrong: R is false, so both 'both true' options are wrong; A is true, so 'A false but R true' is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Separation and isolation of DNA fragments)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Plasmid DNA acts as a vector to transfer the piece of DNA attached to it into the host.
Statement II: Plasmids are linear DNA molecules that replicate only along with the bacterial chromosome.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: plasmid DNA acts as a vector to transfer the piece of DNA attached to it. Plasmids are autonomously replicating, circular, extra-chromosomal DNA; plasmids and bacteriophages can replicate within bacterial cells independent of the control of chromosomal DNA.
steps: Statement II: false - plasmids are circular and replicate independently of the chromosome
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II contradicts both features that make plasmids useful vectors (circular, autonomous replication), while Statement I is NCERT's line.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Principles of Biotechnology; Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Cloning vectors)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A circular vector of 4.4 kb has a single BamHI site. A 1.6 kb DNA fragment with BamHI sticky ends at both ends is ligated into this site. The recombinant plasmid is then completely digested with BamHI. What is the size of the recombinant plasmid, and what does the digestion give?

options.text: 6.0 kb; two fragments, of 4.4 kb and 1.6 kb
4.4 kb; a single fragment of 4.4 kb
6.0 kb; a single linear fragment of 6.0 kb

solution.explanation: Size = 4.4 + 1.6 = 6.0 kb. Inserting a fragment with BamHI ends into the BamHI site recreates a BamHI site at each junction, so the recombinant has two BamHI sites. Cutting a circular DNA at 2 sites gives 2 fragments: the 4.4 kb vector and the 1.6 kb insert.
steps: BamHI sites in the recombinant = 2 (one at each junction)
Circular DNA with n sites -> n fragments -> 4.4 kb and 1.6 kb
solution.why_others_wrong: Three fragments would need three sites (or a linear molecule with two); 4.4 kb ignores the insert; a single 6.0 kb fragment counts only one site in the recombinant.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Restriction enzymes; Cloning vectors)
solution.final_answer: Option B: 6.0 kb; two fragments, of 4.4 kb and 1.6 kb

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
A palindrome in DNA reads the same on the two strands when the orientation of reading is kept the same (5' → 3'). How many of the following double-stranded sequences, each given as its upper (5' → 3') strand, are palindromes?

5'-GTTAAC-3', 5'-CTGCAG-3', 5'-GATATC-3', 5'-AGCTAG-3', 5'-GAACTC-3'

solution.explanation: Write the complementary strand and read it 5' → 3' (that is, take the reverse complement). GTTAAC -> GTTAAC, CTGCAG -> CTGCAG and GATATC -> GATATC are palindromes. AGCTAG -> CTAGCT and GAACTC -> GAGTTC are not.
solution.shortcut: A DNA palindrome equals its own reverse complement.
solution.why_others_wrong: Reading the second strand in the same direction is the test; counting AGCTAG or GAACTC uses the plain complement or a simple reversal instead of the reverse complement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Restriction enzymes)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Three

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: EcoRI recognises 5'-GAATTC-3' (complementary strand 3'-CTTAAG-5') and cuts each strand between the bases G and A. What is the single-stranded overhang on each sticky end produced?

options.text: No overhang, since EcoRI gives blunt ends

solution.explanation: Cutting the upper strand G^AATTC and the lower strand (read 5' → 3', also G^AATTC) leaves each fragment with a single-stranded stretch of 5'-AATT-3'. Because the site is palindromic, both sticky ends carry the same overhang, which is why they can pair with each other by hydrogen bonds.
solution.why_others_wrong: GAAT would need a cut between T and C; a two-base overhang would need a cut in the middle of the other strand; and NCERT shows EcoRI producing sticky, not blunt, ends.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Restriction enzymes)
solution.final_answer: Option A: 5'-AATT-3' on each end

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): During the isolation of DNA, the preparation is treated with ribonuclease.
Reason (R): When the cell is broken open, RNA is released along with DNA, and DNA must be free from other macromolecules before it can be cut with restriction enzymes.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: to cut DNA with restriction enzymes it needs to be in pure form, free from other macromolecules. When the cell is broken open, DNA is released along with other macromolecules such as RNA, proteins, polysaccharides and lipids. RNA is removed by treatment with ribonuclease, proteins with protease. R is the reason for A.
steps: RNA present + DNA must be pure -> RNA removed by ribonuclease -> R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the need to remove RNA is exactly why ribonuclease is used, so B, C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Isolation of the genetic material)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Exonucleases make cuts at specific positions within the DNA, whereas endonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of the DNA.
Statement II: Restriction enzymes belong to a larger class of enzymes called nucleases.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: restriction enzymes belong to a larger class of enzymes called nucleases, of two kinds: exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of the DNA, whereas endonucleases make cuts at specific positions within the DNA. Statement I swaps the two.
steps: Statement I: false - the roles are swapped
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false and Statement II true; the prefix 'endo-' (within) is the clue that endonucleases cut inside the molecule.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Restriction enzymes)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (step or component of PCR) with List-II (what happens or why it is used).

List-I:
A. Denaturation
B. Annealing
C. Extension
D. Thermostable DNA polymerase (from Thermus aquaticus)

List-II:
I. Remains active during the high temperature used to separate the DNA strands
II. DNA polymerase extends the primers using the nucleotides provided and the template DNA
III. Primers bind to complementary regions of the single-stranded template DNA
IV. Double-stranded DNA is separated into single strands by high temperature

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Steps of the polymerase chain reaction
solution.explanation: NCERT: each PCR cycle has three steps: denaturation (high temperature separates the strands), annealing (the two sets of primers bind to complementary regions) and extension (DNA polymerase extends the primers using the nucleotides provided and the genomic DNA as template). A thermostable DNA polymerase, isolated from Thermus aquaticus, is used because it remains active during the high-temperature denaturation.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap denaturation with annealing, annealing with extension, or extension with the reason for using a thermostable enzyme.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Amplification of gene of interest using PCR)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
A restriction digest gives three DNA fragments of 0.5 kb, 2 kb and 5 kb, which are separated by agarose gel electrophoresis. Which of the following are correct?

(a) The 0.5 kb fragment moves farthest from the well.
(b) The 5 kb fragment stays closest to the well.
(c) After staining with ethidium bromide and exposure to UV radiation, three bright orange bands are seen.
(d) The fragments move towards the cathode (negative electrode).
(e) The 2 kb band can be cut out of the gel and the DNA extracted (eluted) for use in constructing recombinant DNA.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: DNA fragments are negatively charged and move towards the anode under an electric field; they separate according to size through the sieving effect of the agarose gel, so the smaller the fragment the farther it moves. Bands are seen after ethidium bromide staining and UV exposure as bright orange bands; the separated bands are cut out and extracted (elution), and the purified fragments are used in constructing recombinant DNA.
solution.why_others_wrong: DNA is negatively charged and moves to the anode, so (d) is false and every option containing it is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Separation and isolation of DNA fragments)
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b), (c) and (e) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Assume a DNA molecule whose sequence is random, with A, T, G and C equally frequent. On average, how many recognition sites of a restriction enzyme that recognises one specific 6-bp palindromic sequence (such as EcoRI's 5'-GAATTC-3') are expected in 409,600 bp of this DNA? (Count along one strand; because the site is palindromic, the other strand gives the same sites.)

solution.explanation: The chance that any given 6 consecutive bases match one specific sequence is (1/4)⁶ = 1/4096. So a 6-bp site is expected about once every 4096 bp. Expected sites = 409,600 / 4096 = 100.
solution.shortcut: A specific n-bp site occurs about once every 4ⁿ bp.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,600 uses a 4-bp site (4⁴ = 256); 25 uses 4⁷; 68,267 divides by 6 instead of by 4⁶.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Restriction enzymes)
solution.final_answer: Option A: 100

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following methods introduce recombinant DNA into host cells WITHOUT using a 'disarmed pathogen' that infects the cell?

(a) Micro-injection of recombinant DNA into the nucleus of an animal cell
(b) Biolistics (gene gun) with DNA-coated gold or tungsten micro-particles
(c) Treatment of bacterial cells with calcium ions followed by a heat shock
(d) Use of the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens
(e) Use of disarmed retroviruses

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Methods of introducing DNA into hosts
solution.explanation: NCERT: in micro-injection recombinant DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell; in biolistics, cells are bombarded with high-velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA (suitable for plants); bacteria are made competent with a divalent cation such as calcium and given a heat shock. The Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium and disarmed retroviruses are 'disarmed pathogen' vectors which, when allowed to infect the cell, transfer the recombinant DNA into the host.
solution.why_others_wrong: Agrobacterium (Ti plasmid) and retroviruses are pathogens modified to be harmless, so they are exactly the 'disarmed pathogen' vectors excluded by the question.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Insertion of recombinant DNA into the host cell/organism)
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In PCR, the DNA polymerase does not have to be added afresh after each denaturation step.
Reason (R): The thermostable DNA polymerase isolated from Thermus aquaticus remains active during the high temperature used for denaturation of double-stranded DNA.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Why a thermostable polymerase is used
solution.explanation: NCERT: the PCR enzyme is a thermostable DNA polymerase (isolated from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus), which remains active during the high temperature induced denaturation of double-stranded DNA. Because the enzyme is not destroyed when the reaction is heated to separate the strands, the same enzyme works through repeated cycles. R explains A.
steps: So it need not be replaced each cycle -> R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: An ordinary polymerase would be inactivated at the denaturation temperature; the thermostability stated in R is exactly why A holds, so B, C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Amplification of gene of interest using PCR)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In PCR, the part of the template that gets amplified is decided by the primers, because the DNA polymerase extends the primers bound to complementary regions of the template.
Statement II: PCR can amplify a gene only after the gene has been cloned in a plasmid and introduced into a living host cell.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: in PCR, multiple copies of the gene (or DNA) of interest are synthesised in vitro using two sets of primers (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to regions of DNA) and the enzyme DNA polymerase, which extends the primers. The primers therefore mark the ends of the amplified region. PCR is done in vitro; its product can later be ligated with a vector for cloning, but no host cell is needed for the amplification.
steps: Statement I: true - amplification runs between the primer-binding regions
Statement II: false - PCR is an in vitro method
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II reverses the order of events: PCR products may be cloned afterwards, but PCR itself needs no living cell.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Amplification of gene of interest using PCR)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (observation after transformation) with List-II (interpretation).

List-I:
A. With a vector carrying ampR and tetR, the insert placed in tetR: a colony grows on ampicillin but not on tetracycline
B. With the same vector: a colony grows on both ampicillin and tetracycline
C. A bacterium spread on an ampicillin plate does not grow at all
D. With a vector whose insert site lies in the β-galactosidase gene: a colony gives no colour with the chromogenic substrate

List-II:
I. Insertional inactivation of the β-galactosidase gene by the insert
II. The cell did not take up the vector
III. Transformant carrying the vector without an insert
IV. Insertional inactivation of the tetracycline resistance gene by the insert

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: normal E. coli cells do not carry resistance against these antibiotics, so a cell that does not grow on ampicillin has not taken up the vector. If foreign DNA is inserted within the tetracycline resistance gene, recombinants lose tetracycline resistance but still grow on ampicillin; non-recombinant transformants grow on both. With β-galactosidase as marker, colonies whose plasmid has an insert give no colour, while those without an insert give blue colonies.
steps: Grows on amp, not tet -> IV
solution.why_others_wrong: Growth on both antibiotics means both genes are intact (no insert), while loss of tetracycline resistance marks the recombinant; a colourless colony marks an insert in the β-galactosidase gene, not a cell without the vector.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Cloning vectors)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A researcher uses a vector whose only selectable marker is the ampicillin resistance gene, but by mistake the E. coli strain used as the host is already resistant to ampicillin. What problem will arise when the treated cells are plated on an ampicillin-containing medium?

options.text: No cells will grow, because the two resistance genes cancel each other
Only the recombinants will grow, because the insert inactivates the host's resistance gene
Non-transformants will also grow, so transformants cannot be distinguished from them
The vector will not replicate, because the host already has an origin of replication

solution.concept: Why the host must lack the marker
solution.explanation: NCERT: selectable markers help in identifying and eliminating non-transformants; antibiotic resistance genes are useful markers for E. coli because normal E. coli cells do not carry resistance against these antibiotics. Only the transformants then grow on the antibiotic. If the host is already resistant, every cell grows, so transformants cannot be told apart from non-transformants.
steps: Selection works only if non-transformants are killed by the antibiotic
Host already resistant -> all cells grow -> no selection
solution.why_others_wrong: Resistance genes do not cancel; the insert sits in the vector, not in the host chromosome; and the vector's ori works independently of the host's own replication.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Cloning vectors)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Non-transformants will also grow, so transformants cannot be distinguished from them

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: NCERT lists several ways in which genetic modification has been useful in crop plants. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.text: Crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses such as cold, drought, salt and heat
Increased efficiency of mineral usage by plants

solution.explanation: NCERT: genetic modification has (i) made crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat), (ii) reduced reliance on chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops), (iii) helped to reduce post-harvest losses, (iv) increased efficiency of mineral usage by plants, and (v) enhanced nutritional value of food, e.g. golden rice.
steps: Listed: stress tolerance, reduced reliance on pesticides, fewer post-harvest losses, better mineral use, better nutrition
Increased reliance on pesticides is the opposite of (ii)
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three are NCERT's own examples of the benefits of GM plants; pest-resistant GM crops reduce, not increase, the use of chemical pesticides.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Biotechnological Applications in Agriculture
solution.final_answer: Option B: Increased reliance on chemical pesticides

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A company wants to introduce a new genetically modified crop for cultivation in India. According to NCERT, which organisation set up by the Indian Government makes decisions regarding the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services?

options.text: The US Patent and Trademark Office

solution.concept: Regulation of GM organisms in India
solution.explanation: NCERT: the Indian Government has set up organisations such as GEAC, which will make decisions regarding the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM-organisms for public services. (NCERT expands GEAC as the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee; the committee is now officially called the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, which is why the option gives only the abbreviation.)
steps: GM organism for public use -> safety and validity decided by GEAC
solution.why_others_wrong: NACO works on AIDS awareness, CDRI developed the pill Saheli, and the US Patent and Trademark Office granted the Basmati patent; none decides on GM organisms in India.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Ethical Issues
solution.final_answer: Option C: GEAC

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (gene or DNA introduced) with List-II (condition it was used to control).

List-I:
A. cryIAc and cryIIAb
B. cryIAb
C. Nematode-specific genes producing sense and anti-sense RNA
D. Functional ADA cDNA

List-II:
I. An immune disorder in a child, treated by gene therapy
II. Infection of tobacco roots by Meloidegyne incognitia
III. Damage by the corn borer
IV. Damage to cotton by bollworms

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: the proteins encoded by cryIAc and cryIIAb control the cotton bollworms, and that of cryIAb controls the corn borer. Nematode-specific genes introduced into tobacco produced sense and anti-sense RNA, which protected the roots from Meloidegyne incognitia by RNAi. A functional ADA cDNA was introduced into the lymphocytes of a child with ADA deficiency (ADA is crucial for the immune system to function).
solution.why_others_wrong: The commonest slip swaps the cotton genes (cryIAc, cryIIAb) with the corn gene (cryIAb); the nematode genes act through RNAi, not as cry toxins.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Biotechnological Applications in Agriculture; Gene Therapy
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about RNA interference (RNAi) are correct according to NCERT?

(a) RNAi takes place in all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defence.
(b) The source of the complementary RNA could be an infection by viruses having RNA genomes.
(c) The source of the complementary RNA could also be mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate.
(d) RNAi is a method of cellular defence found only in prokaryotes.
(e) RNAi works only when the Bt toxin protein is also present in the cell.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: RNAi takes place in all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defence. It involves silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary dsRNA molecule. The source of this complementary RNA could be from an infection by viruses having RNA genomes or mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate. RNAi has nothing to do with the Bt toxin.
steps: (e) false - RNAi and Bt toxin are separate strategies
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) contradicts (a), since NCERT says RNAi occurs in all eukaryotes; (e) mixes up two unrelated pest-resistance methods.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Biotechnological Applications in Agriculture
solution.final_answer: Option C: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Insulin used for diabetes was earlier extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs.
Statement II: About 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human use the world over.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Both are NCERT statements. Insulin was earlier extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs (which caused allergy or other reactions in some patients). NCERT also says that at present about 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human use the world over.
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so any option that calls either of them false is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Biotechnological Applications in Medicine
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (use of transgenic animals) with List-II (reason, as classified in NCERT).

List-I:
A. Transgenic sheep give milk containing a human protein needed to treat a disease
B. Transgenic mice are used, in place of monkeys, to check a new batch of vaccine
C. Transgenic mice made more sensitive to a toxic substance give the results of a drug's toxicity testing in less time
D. Transgenic mice carrying a gene for a human disease are used to try out new treatments

List-II:
I. Study of disease
II. Chemical safety testing
III. Vaccine safety
IV. Biological products

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT gives these reasons: biological products (e.g., human α-1-antitrypsin, human α-lactalbumin in milk); vaccine safety (transgenic mice being developed to test the safety of the polio vaccine, which could replace monkeys); chemical safety testing (animals made more sensitive to toxic substances give results in less time); study of disease (transgenic models to investigate new treatments for human diseases).
solution.why_others_wrong: Each wrong code places a situation under a neighbouring reason; the purpose of the experiment (a product, vaccine checking, toxicity testing or a disease model) decides the category.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Transgenic Animals
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (figure in NCERT) with List-II (what it refers to).

List-I:
A. 1983
B. 1990
C. 27
D. 2.4 grams per litre

List-II:
I. Amount of human protein in the milk of the transgenic cow Rosie
II. Number of documented varieties of Basmati grown in India
III. Year of the first clinical gene therapy, given for ADA deficiency
IV. Year in which Eli Lilly prepared DNA sequences for chains A and B of human insulin and introduced them into plasmids of E. coli

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: in 1983 Eli Lilly prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to chains A and B of human insulin and introduced them into plasmids of E. coli; the first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl with ADA deficiency; there are 27 documented varieties of Basmati grown in India; Rosie, the first transgenic cow (1997), produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre) containing human α-lactalbumin.
solution.why_others_wrong: The two years are the usual mix-up: insulin chains in E. coli came first (1983), gene therapy later (1990); 27 is a count of varieties and 2.4 a concentration, so they cannot be exchanged.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Biotechnological Applications in Medicine; Transgenic Animals; Ethical Issues
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: In the RNAi strategy against Meloidegyne incognitia, suppose that by mistake a gene essential to the tobacco plant itself, rather than a nematode-specific gene, is introduced so that it produces both sense and anti-sense RNA in the plant cells. What is the most likely result?

options.text: The nematode would still be killed, because any dsRNA is toxic to nematodes
Nothing would happen, because RNA interference does not occur in plants
The dsRNA formed would silence the matching mRNA of the tobacco plant, harming the plant rather than the nematode
The plant would become resistant to bollworms, because the dsRNA acts like the Bt toxin

solution.explanation: NCERT: RNAi involves silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary dsRNA molecule that binds to and prevents translation of the mRNA. In the tobacco example the dsRNA was made from nematode genes, so it silenced a specific mRNA of the nematode. RNAi occurs in all eukaryotes, so a dsRNA made from the plant's own gene would silence the matching mRNA of the plant itself.
steps: dsRNA silences the mRNA complementary to it
Plant gene used -> plant mRNA silenced -> plant harmed, nematode not targeted
solution.why_others_wrong: RNAi silences only the mRNA complementary to the dsRNA, so it is not a general nematode poison; RNAi occurs in all eukaryotes, plants included; and dsRNA does not act like the Bt toxin protein.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Biotechnological Applications in Agriculture
solution.final_answer: Option C: The dsRNA formed would silence the matching mRNA of the tobacco plant, harming the plant rather than the nematode

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Bt toxin genes are expressed in crop plants to make them resistant to insect pests.
Reason (R): After being activated by the alkaline pH of the insect gut, the Bt toxin binds to the midgut epithelial cells and creates pores that cause swelling and lysis of the cells, eventually killing the insect.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: Bt toxin genes isolated from Bacillus thuringiensis are incorporated into crop plants such as cotton, providing resistance to insects without the need for insecticides. The toxin kills the insect that eats the plant: the inactive protoxin is solubilised and activated by the alkaline gut pH, binds to the midgut epithelial cells and creates pores, causing swelling and lysis and eventually death. R explains why the expressing crop is resistant.
steps: R: true - the mode of action of Bt toxin
Insect eating the crop is killed -> crop protected -> R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both are NCERT statements, and the killing of feeding insects described in R is what gives the crop its resistance, so B, C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Biotechnological Applications in Agriculture
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
A foreign company uses neem, an Indian traditional herbal medicine, together with the traditional knowledge of the people, to make a commercial product and patents it, without authorisation from India or the people concerned and without any compensatory payment. Which of the following are correct according to NCERT?

(a) NCERT mentions neem among the Indian traditional herbal medicines on which attempts have been made to patent uses, products and processes.
(b) Use of bio-resources in this way, without proper authorisation and compensatory payment, is called biopiracy.
(c) The developing and the under-developed world is rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge related to bio-resources.
(d) Industrialised nations are rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge, so they rarely need bio-resources from other countries.
(e) Biopiracy means using bio-resources only after paying full compensation to the countries concerned.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: there have been attempts to patent uses, products and processes based on Indian traditional herbal medicines, e.g., turmeric and neem. Biopiracy is the term used to refer to the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned and without compensatory payment. Industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge, whereas the developing and under-developed world is rich in them.
steps: (d) false - industrialised nations are poor in biodiversity
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) reverses which nations are rich in biodiversity, and (e) reverses the definition of biopiracy, so any option containing them is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Ethical Issues
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Transgenic mice are being developed for use in testing the safety of the polio vaccine.
Reason (R): Over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Both are NCERT statements. The reason given for A is vaccine safety: if successful, transgenic mice could replace monkeys for testing the safety of batches of the polio vaccine. R is a separate fact about how common transgenic mice are; it does not explain why they are used to test the polio vaccine.
steps: R does not give the reason for A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both are true, so C and D are wrong; the share of mice among transgenic animals is a different fact and not the reason for using them in vaccine testing, so A is also wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Transgenic Animals
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the gene therapy given for ADA deficiency, lymphocytes from the patient's blood were grown in a culture outside the body.
Statement II: The functional ADA cDNA was introduced into these lymphocytes by biolistics (gene gun).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: in gene therapy for ADA deficiency, lymphocytes from the blood of the patient are grown in a culture outside the body; a functional ADA cDNA is then introduced into these lymphocytes using a retroviral vector, and the cells are returned to the patient.
steps: Statement II: false - a retroviral vector was used, not biolistics
solution.why_others_wrong: Biolistics is described in NCERT as a method suited to plant cells; the ADA cDNA was delivered by a retroviral vector, so Statement II is false and Statement I true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Gene Therapy
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A tomato crop is badly damaged by beetles (coleopterans). Following NCERT's account of Bt crops, which transgenic approach would be most suitable?

options.text: Express cryIAc and cryIIAb, since these genes control every kind of insect
Introduce nematode-specific genes so that RNAi silences the beetles' mRNA
Express in tomato the toxin gene from a strain of Bacillus thuringiensis whose protein kills coleopterans
Introduce the genes used in golden rice, since vitamin A protects plants from beetles

solution.concept: Choosing Bt toxin genes for a target pest
solution.explanation: NCERT: some strains of Bacillus thuringiensis produce proteins that kill certain insects such as lepidopterans, coleopterans (beetles) and dipterans; most Bt toxins are insect-group specific, and the choice of genes depends upon the crop and the targeted pest. Bt toxin genes have been expressed in tomato among other crops. So the tomato should be given toxin genes from a strain whose protein kills coleopterans.
steps: Choose genes from a strain toxic to coleopterans and express them in tomato
solution.why_others_wrong: cryIAc and cryIIAb are named for cotton bollworms, and Bt toxins are not effective against every insect; RNAi with nematode genes would target a nematode, not beetles; golden rice genes improve nutrition, not pest resistance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Biotechnological Applications in Agriculture
solution.final_answer: Option C: Express in tomato the toxin gene from a strain of Bacillus thuringiensis whose protein kills coleopterans

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Suppose that, instead of following Eli Lilly's approach, a company expressed in E. coli a single gene for human pro-insulin. Based on NCERT, what additional step would be needed to obtain functional insulin?

options.text: Addition of a C peptide, which mature insulin requires
Separation of chains A and B so that they are never joined
Conversion of the protein into DNA before injection
Removal of the C peptide, to convert the pro-hormone into mature insulin

solution.explanation: NCERT: in mammals, including humans, insulin is synthesised as a pro-hormone which contains an extra stretch called the C peptide; this C peptide is not present in mature insulin and is removed during maturation into insulin. The main challenge was getting insulin assembled into a mature form, which Eli Lilly avoided by making chains A and B separately and joining them by disulphide bonds. A pro-insulin product would still need its C peptide removed.
steps: Mature insulin lacks the C peptide
So the C peptide must be removed
solution.why_others_wrong: The C peptide is absent from mature insulin, so it must be removed, not added; chains A and B must be linked (by disulphide bridges) in functional insulin; and a protein is not converted into DNA.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Biotechnological Applications in Medicine (Genetically Engineered Insulin)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Removal of the C peptide, to convert the pro-hormone into mature insulin

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (problem) with List-II (solution described in NCERT).

List-I:
A. Some patients developed allergy to insulin from slaughtered cattle and pigs
B. Genetically engineered lymphocytes are not immortal, so infusions must be repeated
C. Emphysema patients need human α-1-antitrypsin
D. People eating mainly rice may lack vitamin A

List-II:
I. Golden rice
II. Transgenic animals producing the human protein
III. Introducing the ADA gene into cells at early embryonic stages
IV. Human insulin produced by recombinant DNA technology

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: animal insulin caused allergy or other reactions in some patients, a problem avoided by recombinant human insulin; lymphocyte-based ADA therapy needs periodic infusion because the cells are not immortal, while introducing the gene from ADA-producing marrow cells into cells at early embryonic stages could be a permanent cure; transgenic animals have been used to make human α-1-antitrypsin used to treat emphysema; golden rice is a GM crop enriched in vitamin A.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes give the insulin problem the transgenic-animal solution, give the lymphocyte problem a protein product instead of early embryonic gene introduction, or exchange golden rice with α-1-antitrypsin.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Biotechnological Applications in Medicine; Gene Therapy; Transgenic Animals
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A patent is the right granted by a government to an inventor to prevent others from commercial use of his invention.
Statement II: There is a growing realisation of the injustice, inadequate compensation and benefit sharing between developed and developing countries.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Both are NCERT statements. A patent is a right granted by a government to an inventor to prevent others from commercial use of the invention. In its discussion of biopiracy, NCERT also notes a growing realisation of the injustice, inadequate compensation and benefit sharing between developed and developing countries.
steps: Statement I: true - definition of a patent
Statement II: true - injustice and inadequate benefit sharing
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are NCERT's own lines, so no option calling either false is correct.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Ethical Issues
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements correctly compare Bt cotton with the RNAi-based tobacco that resists Meloidegyne incognitia?

(a) In Bt cotton the protective molecule is a protein, whereas in the RNAi tobacco it is a double-stranded RNA.
(b) The genes used in Bt cotton come from a bacterium, whereas those used in the RNAi tobacco come from the pest (the nematode) itself.
(c) Vectors derived from Agrobacterium were used to introduce the nematode-specific genes into tobacco.
(d) Both strategies work by silencing a specific mRNA of the pest.
(e) Both strategies kill the pest by creating pores in the cells of its midgut.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: Bt cotton expresses cry genes isolated from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis; the toxin protein kills insects by binding to midgut epithelial cells and making pores. In the tobacco example, nematode-specific genes were introduced into the host plant using Agrobacterium vectors; they produced sense and anti-sense RNA, which formed dsRNA that silenced a specific mRNA of the nematode (RNAi).
steps: (b) true - bacterial genes vs nematode genes
(e) false - only the Bt toxin forms pores
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) applies only to RNAi and (e) only to the Bt toxin; each wrongly extends one mechanism to both crops.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Biotechnological Applications in Agriculture
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only
